# Release Notes

Curated release notes for `@malloy-publisher/sdk`, `@malloy-publisher/app`, `@malloy-publisher/server`, and `@malloy-publisher/cli` (versioned in lockstep).

## How this file is used

The `Release (NPM + Docker)` workflow (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) creates GitHub releases automatically with a standard header (NPM/Docker links) plus an auto-generated "What's Changed" PR list via `gh release create --generate-notes`. That auto list is sufficient for routine patch releases.

For releases that warrant narrative — redesigns, breaking changes, migration steps — write a `## [Unreleased] — an entry file that reaches a stored base through an import serves it

**[fix] A stored source is served from its table through an entry file that reaches it only through a file it imports.** Take `#(materialize) activity_events` in `activity.malloy`, `org_activity is activity_events extend { … }` in `eng.malloy`, and an `index.malloy` that imports only `eng.malloy`. That is the usual shape of a published surface. Malloy imports are not transitive, and an extension of a table-backed source records no link to its base, so `index.malloy`'s compile held nothing that pointed back to `activity_events`.

Three things went wrong as a result:
- its served copy re-rooted nothing, and every query on `org_activity` through `index.malloy` was answered live, with no warning;
- the package also warned `materialization-unreachable` about `activity_events`, although a published source reads it;
- where the entry file reached one stored source and not another, its copy could fail to compile with `cross_connection_unbuilt`.

The served copy now finds such a base the way it finds a kept block's base: from the declaring file's text. It re-roots the base in its own file, and proves the result through the sources the entry file names over it. Two limits:
- **A stored base that filters its own rows** (a `where:` it declares or inherits) is still answered live through such an entry file, as before.
- **A source the entry file declares itself that joins such an extension** can now be warned `served-copy-not-served` (`cross_connection_join`) when the stored table is in a storage destination its own connection cannot reach. That source answers live, as it always did.

**Who is affected:** packages whose `index.malloy` imports the files that extend a stored source, but not the file that stores it. **What to do:** nothing; the workaround of importing every file into `index.malloy` is no longer needed.

## [Unreleased]` section below, in the PR that changes the behaviour. **The release workflow does almost all of the rest**: `prepare` restamps every `[Unreleased]` heading with the release's version on the `release/v<version>` branch it publishes from, in the same commit as the version bump, and `gh-release` appends those sections to the release page alongside the generated PR list. Nothing to paste, and nothing to remember while writing.

One step is a human's: someone has to open `release/v<version>` as a PR into `main` and merge it. `main` requires a pull request, so the release cannot land it itself, and the job summary prints the link. Until it merges the headings on `main` still read `[Unreleased]` and the next release would ship them twice, so the `Release sync` check (`release-sync.yml`) fails on `main` and on every pull request until it does. Whoever cuts the release owns that PR; the `publisher-release` skill makes it a step.

Both steps handle several sections, which matters because unrelated narratives accumulate between releases: they are separate entries in the same release rather than alternatives. That is precisely what the old manual process got wrong. It also simply stopped happening — 0.0.243 through 0.0.247 each shipped with none of their narrative, and the pages were backfilled by hand afterwards.

Give the heading a title — `## [Unreleased] — what changed`, with an em dash, a colon or a hyphen. The version is already the release's own title, so the marker is stripped and the title is what appears on the page; a bare `## [Unreleased]` has nothing to put there and fails CI on the PR that writes it.

Two consequences worth knowing. A section merged to `main` ships in the **next** release, whenever that is, so do not write one for work that has not landed. And a heading already stamped with a version is history: a follow-up that changes that behaviour opens a **new** `[Unreleased]` section referencing the shipped version by number, rather than editing the old one.

## [Unreleased] — breaking: skill sets and workflows replace package agents, a package's own skills live in the `default` skill set, a `SKILL.md` is served as written, and `agents` and a root `skills/` are no longer read

**Breaking: a package declares `skillSets` and `workflows`, not `agents`.** `skillSets` in `publisher.json` is an object keyed by set name, `{ path, description?, overrides? }`, where `path` is a package-relative folder whose subfolders are skills (`<path>/<skill>/SKILL.md`). A set's name is its key, whatever its folder is called. An entry under `workflows` is a named job, `{ description?, instructions, skillSets? }`: `instructions` is required (a `.md` file in the package, at most 16 KiB) and `skillSets` lists at most 8 names of declared sets. A name is 1 to 64 lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, and a package declares at most 32 sets and 64 workflows. A key Publisher does not know, a bad name, a bad path, or a workflow that lists a set nobody declares refuses that one entry with a load warning, and the others keep serving; a key starting `x-` is ignored. Two sets declared at one path are both refused. Every declared set is read once per load, served whole at its own route whether or not a workflow lists it, and shared by every workflow that lists it. A skill name that two of one workflow's sets both hold comes back from both, with a `skill-shadowed` warning on the workflow, and an installer keeps the first-listed set's copy. Publisher still serves a definition and never runs one: adopt a workflow only when the user names it.

**Breaking: the `default` skill set is the package's own skills.** The skills in `skillSets.default`, beside the bundled ones, are what `get_skill`, `get_context` and the `…/skills` routes advertise. A package that declares no `default` set has no skills of its own, which is what a root `skills/` directory used to give it. A `default` skill named like a bundled skill replaces it only when `default`'s `overrides` lists the name; otherwise the bundled skill is served and the set carries a finding that names the fix. A set read or a workflow read serves the set whole whatever `overrides` says. Only `default`'s `overrides` is read: on any other set it is ignored, with a finding. The `malloy-` and `eval-` prefixes belong to the skills Publisher bundles, and a future bundled skill may take any name under them, so a new bundled skill name counts as a breaking change from here on, since a package skill that already has it stops being served unless `overrides` lists it. Credible's agent keeps its own copy of a bundled skill and skips a package skill of that name.

**Breaking: `agents` and a root `skills/` are no longer read.** A manifest that declares `agents` loads with a warning that says to declare `workflows` instead and points at the migration section of the packages guide (`package-agents-not-read`). A package with a root `skills/` directory that no declared skill set is at or under loads with a warning that names the one-line fix, `"skillSets": { "default": { "path": "skills" } }`, with `overrides` for a skill that replaces a bundled one and a `.skillignore` for what a skill must not serve (`package-skills-dir-not-read`). The package still loads, its models still serve, and each such load or reload is counted in `publisher_deprecated_usage_total` (features `agents` and `skills_dir`). Before you deploy, find the affected packages by scanning stored packages for an `agents` key in `publisher.json` or a root `skills/` folder: `publisher_deprecated_usage_total` counts loads, not packages, so it cannot list them. After the upgrade, the two codes on a package's `warnings` name each one. `schedules`, `budget`, `model` and tasks are gone with agents: nothing ran a schedule, and nothing here sets a model or a budget. A recurring job needs a scheduler of your own that fetches the workflow.

A published version is immutable, so a version with a root `skills/` serves no package skills on this release until it is republished with the one-line declaration. The declaration changes two things a root folder never had: a skill named like a bundled skill replaces it only if `default`'s `overrides` lists the name, and every file of a skill is served now, so a file it must not serve goes in a `.skillignore`. Reading a root `skills/` as an implicit `default` is refused because a root folder that replaces bundled skills with no declaration is what `overrides` exists to end, and an implicit `default` would give a package two ways to declare one set.

**Breaking: a `SKILL.md` is served as written, on every route, and an installer writes only `name` and `description`.** `get_skill`, `…/skills/{skill}` and the set and workflow reads return a skill's `SKILL.md` byte for byte, with its `name` and `description` also on the entry. No route strips a key, so an author's `allowed-tools` or `hooks` reaches whoever installs the file unchanged. The install rule is what protects an installing user: write only `name` and `description` into the installed file's frontmatter, taken from the entry's own fields (the description JSON-quoted), then the text after the file's frontmatter, and name any other key the file carried to the user. The `get_workflow` and `get_skill_set` descriptions state it and the bundled `malloy-run-workflow` skill does it, and never overwrites a skill the user already has. Publishing is unauthenticated, so on a shared Publisher an installer that keeps a file's frontmatter gives up the bounded reader's protection (the server's own size-capped, expansion-limited read of it, whose `name` and `description` the installer writes instead of parsing the file's own); see `docs/security-posture.md`.

**Breaking: the REST, MCP and SDK surfaces.** `get_agent`, `GET …/agents`, `GET …/agents/{name}` and `GET …/agents/{name}/skills/{path}` are removed, as are the `AgentSummary`, `Agent`, `AgentSchedule` and `AgentBudget` schemas, `asset_roots` and `asset_counts`, and the `agents` field of `Package`. In their place: MCP `get_workflow(workflow?, skills?)` and `get_skill_set(skill_set?, skills?, skill_path?)`; `GET …/skill-sets` (`SkillSetSummary[]`), `GET …/skill-sets/{name}` (`SkillSet`; `?skills=summary` leaves out file text and the set's `assets`) and `GET …/skill-sets/{name}/skills/{path}` (a `<skill>/<file>` path); `GET …/workflows` (`WorkflowSummary[]`, each with `skill_set_names`) and `GET …/workflows/{name}` (`Workflow`, with the instructions and each listed set whole). A set is read through the set routes and `get_skill_set`. The SDK's `ServerProvider` carries `workflows` and `skillSets` where it carried `agents`, and the package page lists skill sets (`default` first, marked always on) and workflows. The bundled skills `malloy-define-agent` and `malloy-run-agent` are replaced by `malloy-define-workflow` and `malloy-run-workflow`. The generated schemas are renamed to match: `AgentSkillFile`, `AgentAsset`, `AgentSkillRead` and `AgentSource` are `SkillSetFile`, `SkillSetAsset`, `SkillSetFileRead` and `ServedSource`, and the SDK's generated `AgentsApi` is `WorkflowsApi`, beside a new `SkillSetsApi`. The SDK's generated `PackageWarningsInner`, the inline type of an entry of `Package.warnings`, is now `PackageWarning`, which `Workflow.warnings` and `SkillSet.warnings` share.

**Changed: `get_workflow` and `get_skill_set` hold their reply to 35,000 characters, Cursor's limit.** A full view that does not fit comes back as the summary view (each skill file as its size, name and description, with no listed files). A summary that still does not fit keeps a workflow's instructions and each set's `name` and `digest`, or a set's `name`, `digest` and `source`, and drops the skill entries and `warnings`. A workflow that still does not fit keeps only its `name` and `source`. Each of these carries a `message` that says so and names the REST read, which has no such limit; a file that does not fit comes back as its message alone.

**Changed: budgets are per skill set.** Each set has 256 KiB and at most 1,000 files of inline Markdown, at most 64 skills, and 4 MiB and 200 listed files; the 8 MiB cap on listed files is charged set by set in name order, so a set that would cross it is refused whole, and so is every workflow that lists it. A bad skill, a skill directory whose name has a control character, `..` or a character outside `[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9._-]*` (or that differs from another skill's only by case, the second being skipped), a strict finding under `assets/` (a link, `..`, a case collision, a `SKILL.md`), a `publisher.json` inside a skill, a skill whose `assets/` the search for a `publisher.json` cannot finish within the set's 10,000-entry budget (it counts every entry it lists, and sets aside the skill that runs it out and each later skill of the set with anything under `assets/`), or a `SKILL.md` that does not fit the set's inline budget is skipped with a finding on its set, and the set still serves. A `publisher.json` at or above a set's root refuses the set. A set that fails to read makes every set and workflow unavailable (see below). "Budgets" in `docs/agent-skills/authoring-skills.md` has every limit.

**Changed: digests.** A set's `digest` covers each served file's path and as-written SHA-256, each skill's applied `.skillignore` and the set's sorted `overrides`; it does not cover the set's name, path or description, so two sets with the same content have the same digest. A workflow's `definitionSha` covers its name, description, the SHA-256 of its instructions and each listed set's `name` and `digest`, in order. `sourceContentSha` covers the models, the `skillSets` and `workflows` declaration and every file a served set or workflow reads, as written. Editing one set leaves every other set's `digest` alone, and a `SKILL.md` served as written means every byte of it moves the `digest`. Both the `get_skill_set` and `get_workflow` replies carry `source` shas that pin what was read.

**Changed: skill sets and workflows are walked in the package-load worker, and a walk that fails answers 409.** A package's sets and workflows are read and hashed in the worker that compiles its models, so a package with large skill sets no longer holds the event loop on creation or on every reload: at the most a package may declare (32 sets, every per-set cap spent), the main thread pays about 20 ms to receive and adopt the result and the worker about 2.3 s, which counts against `packageLoad.jobTimeoutMs`. "What a reload costs" in `docs/agent-skills/authoring-skills.md` has the measured rows. If the load cannot read a package's skill sets or an instructions file (the walk threw, or a listed set or file cannot be read: `EACCES`, `EIO`), the models still load, one `skill-sets-unavailable` warning names the cause, and every `…/skill-sets` and `…/workflows` route, `get_skill_set` and `get_workflow` answer 409 with `reason: SKILL_SETS_UNAVAILABLE` and the cause, until the package reloads; there is no `Retry-After`. So do the `…/skills` routes and `get_skill`, and `get_context` adds a note, when the package declares a `default` set, even for a bundled skill's name, because a `default` skill can replace a bundled one; a package without one serves the bundled skills as usual. A name the manifest never declares is still a 404. A set also holds at most 64 skill directories (the first 64 by name are served, with one finding) and names at most 20 skill findings and at most 20 skipped files, each followed by one line counting the rest.

**Changed: warnings carry a code and a subject, and a 404 says why.** Every finding of a set or a workflow is a `PackageWarning` (`message`, `severity`, `code`, `subject`) on `Package.warnings`, and `SkillSet.warnings` and `Workflow.warnings` carry the same objects. The codes are `workflow-not-served` and `skill-set-not-served` (`subject` the workflow's or set's name), `skill-shadowed` (the workflow's name), `skill-file-skipped` and `skill-finding` (the set's name) and `skill-sets-unavailable` (no subject), so a client no longer reads an English prefix. A set or workflow that is not found answers with a `reason`: `SKILL_SET_NOT_SERVED` or `WORKFLOW_NOT_SERVED` when the manifest declares it and Publisher refuses it (the message is the refusal), `SKILL_SET_NOT_DECLARED` or `WORKFLOW_NOT_DECLARED` when it declares no such name. A `skillSets` or `workflows` value that is refused whole (not an object, over its count, over 1 MiB together or too deeply nested) answers every name `*_NOT_SERVED`, with the text of the package warning that says so, which carries no `code`. Each refused set and workflow is logged once per load at `warn`. `PackageWarning.message` is required. Findings read plainer: sizes print as KiB and MiB, not bytes; a directory with no `SKILL.md` says it has none; a folder that holds a `SKILL.md` and is declared as a set says it is a skill, names the parent folder to declare, and says to remove the `SKILL.md` if its subfolders are the skills; a link loop or a too-long name at a set's root says so, not "does not exist", and the same in an instructions file, a `SKILL.md` or a reference says "does not exist", "is part of a link loop" or "has a name that is too long", not "cannot be read (…)"; and a shadowed skill name and frontmatter read line by line end in a `Fix:` line.

**Changed: watch mode recompiles for a manifest edit, and a burst of file events runs one reload.** A package's own `publisher.json` now recompiles the package when it changes, since it declares the sets and workflows, as does a `publisher.json` that appears in a skill set's folder or above it, which refuses the set. A `.json` file elsewhere is still only a live-reload event. A checkout that touches hundreds of files used to queue one reload per event and run them one after another; each package now has one reload running and at most one pending, which re-runs once for every event that arrived while it ran.

**Skills and server are two installs, and either can be the newer.** An installed `malloy-run-agent` from the last release calls `get_agent`, which this release removes, so its recipe no longer matches the server; update the skills with the server. A `malloy-run-workflow` from this release against an older server finds no `get_skill_set` tool and stops at its third step, saying the server serves no package workflows, without reading or installing anything. Upgrade a host's skills and its server together.

**Who is affected:** a package that declares `agents` or keeps skills in a root `skills/`, a package whose own skill shares a name with a bundled skill, and a client that calls `get_agent`, the `…/agents` routes or the SDK's `agents` client. **What to do:** move each agent task into its own workflow, and the skills into skill sets:

- A task becomes a workflow whose `instructions` is the task file (`weekly-report.md` becomes `workflows.weekly-report`).
- An agent's own `instructions` become a skill, with a one-sentence `description` saying when to read it, in a set the workflow lists.
- Root `skills/<x>/` stay in place when `default` is declared with `"skillSets": { "default": { "path": "skills" } }`, the one-line fix. Moving them to `skill_sets/default/<x>/` is only for tidiness.
- A `default` skill that shares a name with a bundled skill needs the name in `default`'s `overrides` to keep replacing it, or a new name.
- An agent's `instructions` reached every session; a skill is read when its `description` matches, and a workflow's `instructions` only when a user names it. Guidance that must still reach every session goes in a skill of the `default` set.
- Delete `agents/` and the old `skills/` in the same change.

Before:

```json
{
  "name": "storefront",
  "agents": {
    "analyst": {
      "description": "Answers revenue questions using the storefront conventions",
      "instructions": "agents/analyst/instructions.md",
      "skills": ["agents/analyst/skills"],
      "schedules": [{ "cron": "0 13 * * MON", "task": "agents/analyst/tasks/weekly-report.md" }],
      "budget": { "turns": 30 }
    }
  }
}
```

with `skills/storefront-conventions/SKILL.md` beside it. After:

```json
{
  "name": "storefront",
  "skillSets": {
    "default": { "path": "skill_sets/default" },
    "analyst": { "path": "skill_sets/analyst" }
  },
  "workflows": {
    "weekly-report": {
      "description": "Writes the weekly storefront report as the analyst",
      "instructions": "workflows/weekly-report/instructions.md",
      "skillSets": ["analyst", "default"]
    }
  }
}
```

with `skill_sets/default/storefront-conventions/SKILL.md`, `workflows/weekly-report/instructions.md` (the old task file) and `skill_sets/analyst/analyst-guidance/SKILL.md` (the old agent `instructions`, beside the skills from `agents/analyst/skills`).

## [Unreleased] — a skill is its whole directory, and `.skillignore` decides which files an agent is given

**New: a skill ships every file under its directory.** A package's skills (`skills/<x>/`) and the skills an agent named used to serve `SKILL.md`, a flat `reference/*.md` and, for an agent, `assets/**`; `scripts/`, `references/` and every other file were left out, so editing one moved no sha. Now a skill, which lives in a skill set, is its whole directory, as the [Agent Skills spec](https://agentskills.io) lays it out. Markdown outside `assets/` is carried inline in the set's reply (its `skills`, at any depth, within the set's 256 KiB inline budget). Every other file is listed in the set's `assets` with its path, size and sha256, and served on request: a text file as `file_contents`, a binary file as a `message` with no bytes. Markdown that does not fit the inline budget, or is not UTF-8, is listed instead of dropped. A set lists files against budgets of its own (4 MiB and 200 files per set, and 8 MiB across the package). Every limit is in "Budgets" in `docs/agent-skills/authoring-skills.md`, and each crossing is a load warning that names the file.

**New: `.skillignore`.** A `.skillignore` at a skill's root (gitignore syntax, matched without regard to case) drops files from the skill: the files it lists, hashes, serves and installs. Dotfiles, `node_modules/`, `__pycache__/` and `*.pyc` are never part of a skill, and a `SKILL.md` below the root, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `AGENTS.md` and `publisher.json` are skipped with a warning wherever they sit in a skill. A `publisher.json` at the skill's root, in `reference/` or `references/`, or below `assets/`, and a `SKILL.md` below `assets/`, set the whole skill aside with a finding on its set, and the set still serves; a `SKILL.md` below `assets/` that `.skillignore` or a budget hides is not refused, since nothing reads it. An ignored file is still in the package, so `.skillignore` is curation and not a way to hide a secret. Its size is bounded because every pattern runs against every path the walk examines: at most 16 KiB, 50 patterns, 200 characters each and 1,024 together, and two `*` or `**` segments a pattern; a pattern past a bound is skipped with a warning. A path from a skill's root is limited to 200 characters (a longer entry is skipped with one warning, and a directory that long is not descended), because a pattern with a slash backtracks across every segment of the path it is matched against; a listed file over that was already refused, so the one change to what is served is inline Markdown with a path over 200 characters, which is now skipped. Ignored entries count toward the 1,000-entry walk limit, and a Markdown file in a skill's `reference/` or `references/` counts toward its 1,000 whether or not `.skillignore` matches it. See "Which files a skill holds" in `docs/packages.md`. `@malloy-publisher/skills` uses it: its 33 `*_test.py` files and three of `malloy-excel-review`'s four fixture files no longer ship.

**Changed: a block-scalar `description` parses to its true length.** The frontmatter is read as YAML 1.2, so `description: >-` or `|` is the whole text and not its first line. That can push a package past the 4,000-character skill listing that a host such as an agent computer applies, and the host then refuses the skills; shorten the description. A frontmatter that does not parse, repeats a key, is over 4 KiB, references one anchor more than 100 times, or expands past 5 times its source plus 10,000 characters is served as an empty `frontmatter` with `name` and `description` read line by line, and a warning.

**Changed: what a skill's `reference/` serves.** `references/`, the spec's name, is read exactly like `reference/`. Each serves at most 1,000 Markdown files, and Publisher reads no further than 10,000 entries of any kind, so a `reference/` holding more than 10,000 entries can lose Markdown that was served before, and which files stay follows filesystem order. A dot-named file there (`reference/.x.md`) is no longer served. A `.md` file that is not UTF-8 is listed, not inlined, with a warning; a skill whose `SKILL.md` is not UTF-8 is skipped with a warning.

**Changed: a reload reads and hashes every listed file.** A skill set's `digest`, a workflow's `definitionSha` and the package's `sourceContentSha` cover them and each applied `.skillignore`, and `sourceContentSha` hashes each inline Markdown file by the digest taken when it was loaded instead of reading it a second time. The walk and hash run in the package-load worker on load and on every reload; "What a reload costs" in `docs/agent-skills/authoring-skills.md` has the measured time, and a set serves at most 64 skills, so the time has a ceiling.

## [Unreleased] — breaking: `get_skill` addresses a file by `path`, `<skill>/<stem>` is gone, the skill route reads only `SKILL.md`, and `content` is the file as written

**Breaking: `get_skill`.** It takes `path`, relative to the skill root and defaulting to `SKILL.md`, in place of the `<skill>/<stem>` name for a reference file (`get_skill("house-rules/margin")` is now `get_skill("house-rules", "reference/margin.md")`). A read returns `skill: {name, path, content?, size?, origin?, frontmatter?, files?}`: `content` is the file as written (no licence header stripped, no generated section appended), so a `SKILL.md`'s `content` now includes its frontmatter, and `SKILL.md` also returns the parsed `frontmatter` and `files`, every file of the skill as `{path, size}`. `availableSkills` comes back only on a listing or for a name that does not exist, no longer on every call, and `skill` is absent, not `null`, when nothing was read. A binary file returns its `size` and a message; a bundled skill's non-Markdown file returns its size and says to install `@malloy-publisher/skills`. A reply is held to 35,000 characters, Cursor's limit: past it `files` is trimmed with a count, then the parsed frontmatter is dropped, then the body; a listing or an unknown-name reply drops guides from the end, with a count, except that a scoped one keeps the package's own guides first.

**Breaking: the REST routes.** `GET …/packages/{pkg}/skills/{skill}` reads `SKILL.md`, with its `frontmatter` and `files`. `…/skills/{skill}/{stem}` answers 404, as does any path after the skill name. `content` is verbatim, and the `Skill` schema gains `path`, `frontmatter` and `files`. A package skill's other files have one REST read, the skill-set route: `GET …/skill-sets/{set}/skills/{skill}/{file}`, and the `default` set's skills are read at `…/skill-sets/default/skills/…`. A bundled skill's other files are read only through MCP `get_skill(skill, path)`. A listed file that changed on disk since the package loaded answers 404 on the set route until the package reloads.

**Breaking: MCP prompts.** There is one prompt per bundled skill, its `SKILL.md` body. The per-reference prompts (`<skill>/<stem>`) are gone: a client that called one reads the file with `get_skill(skill_name, path)`.

**Bundled skills: eight files are split to fit the budget, each keeping its path.** The part that moved is in a new file beside it, with a pointer left behind: `malloy-excel-review/reference/cookbook-lookup-aggregate-2.md`, `cookbook-pivot-2.md`, `cookbook-scenario-2.md` and `translate-formulas-2.md`; `eval-answer/reference/ledger-schema-events.md`; `malloy-model/reference/legacy-filter.md` and `joined-source-template.md`; `malloy-gotchas-modeling/reference/relative-data-paths.md` and `json-files.md`; and `eval-loop/reference/scrape-minimally.md`.

**An installed copy of the old `malloy-run-agent` recipe stops at its third step.** Step 2 calls `get_agent`, which this Publisher no longer has, and step 3 tells the agent that the server is older than package agents ("this server serves no package agents") and to stop: it reads no definition and installs nothing. The message misnames the cause, since this server is newer. Installed copies come from `@malloy-publisher/skills` on npm, `cred setup` and the plugins, and updating the skills replaces `malloy-run-agent` with `malloy-run-workflow`, whose recipe pins each read to the definition's `source.versionId`, writes each listed file to a temporary file, moves it into place only when `file_contents` came back and its SHA-256 is the listed one, and tells the agent to copy a binary file from the package.

**Skills and server are two installs, and either can be the newer.** A skill from this release that reads a file with `get_skill(skill, path)` against an older server gets `SKILL.md` back, because the older server ignores `path`; each bundled skill that does this tells the agent to check that the reply's `skill.path` is the path it asked for, and to treat anything else as a file not read. An older skill against this server passes a `<skill>/<stem>` name and gets a message that no guide has that name and that a file is read with `skill_name` plus `path`: nothing is read, and the reply says why. Upgrade a host's skills and its server together.

**Who is affected:** a client that calls `get_skill` or the skill routes, reads `availableSkills` from every reply, or calls a per-reference prompt. **What to do:** pass the file's path instead of a `<skill>/<stem>` name, read `content` as the file itself, and update installed skills.

## [Unreleased] — an inherited `where:` that cannot be verified says so

**[new] A query denied because a `where:` its source inherits could not be verified now answers with its own reason and says why.** Publisher checks, on every query, that a `where:` a source inherits from a source it is built from still reads the fields it was written against. Until now a failed check answered `403`, `reason: ACCESS_DENIED`, `Access denied for source "…"`, exactly like a gate's denial, and logged its reason only at debug level. An author whose model was denied this way could not tell it from a permission rule. The deny itself is unchanged, and it still fails closed with the same status. Two things change:

- **The response:** `reason: INHERITED_FILTER_UNVERIFIED`. The message names the source and a reason class (`redefined_field`, `unrecorded_join`, `unresolved_declaration` or `resolution_bound`), and says it is not a permission rule. It never names the filter or the file.
- **The server:** logs one info line, `Inherited where: could not be verified; denying`, with the model, source, filter text, declaring source and file. A new counter, `publisher_inherited_filter_unverified_total{reason}`, counts these denials.

**Who is affected:** clients that branch on `reason: ACCESS_DENIED`. This denial no longer carries it, so treat `INHERITED_FILTER_UNVERIFIED` as a model problem, not a permission one; supplying givens does not help. The access record still books it as `denied_filter`, and `publisher_authorize_row_level_total{decision="denied_by_gate"}` still counts it. **What to do:** to find one of these denials, search the server log for the info line above.

## [Unreleased] — an inherited `where:` checked against the right source on a stored table

**[fix] A source whose `where:` it inherits from a stored source in another file is no longer denied through an entry file that imports both files.** Take `deals is deals_including_deleted extend { where: not is_deleted }` in `deals.malloy`, with `deals_including_deleted` stored; `funnel_deals is deals extend { … }` in `funnel.malloy`; and an `index.malloy` that imports both. Once the stored table was bound, every query on `funnel_deals` through `index.malloy` answered `Access denied for source "funnel_deals"`. Live, and through `funnel.malloy`, the same query answered. The check that an inherited `where:` still reads the fields it was written against took `funnel_deals`'s own declaration from another compile as the source the `where:` was declared on. That declaration reads the original fields while the served one reads the stored table, so the two never matched. It now checks the `where:` against the source that declares it. **Who is affected:** packages whose entry file imports both a stored base's file and a file that extends it; this has happened since at least 0.18.3. **What to do:** nothing. The workaround of extending the stored source directly is no longer needed.

**[fix] The same check no longer lets a redefinition through on that path.** For the same reason, a source that redefines a field an inherited `where:` reads, queried the same way, was answered from the stored table, where live denies it. It is now denied there too, as it is live. **Who is affected:** packages that redefine (`except:` and declare again) a field a base's `where:` reads. **What to do:** nothing, unless such a source was being queried this way; it now answers `Access denied`, as it always did live.

## [Unreleased] — a stored extension of a base in another file serves the base's joins

**[fix] A `#(materialize)` extension of a base declared in another file is served from its table when that base joins a source its own file imports.** Take `#(materialize) activity is activity_base extend { … }`, where `activity_base` is declared in `base.malloy` and joins `users`, which `base.malloy` imports from `users.malloy`. The served copy compiles `activity_base`'s `extend` block again in `activity`'s file, and `users` is no name there, because Malloy imports are not transitive. So the block was not carried: the source warned `served-copy-not-served` (`fields_not_carried`), and every query on it answered live, in its own file and in every file that imports it. The served copy now imports `users` into its copy of that file, selectively, from the file that declares it, and serves the source from its table. It does this only when the name is not already bound in that file; a name already bound there must bind to the same source as in the base's file, or the block is still not carried. That also covers a base imported selectively (`import { activity_base } from "base.malloy"`), which was never carried before. **Who is affected:** packages that store an extension of a base from another file whose `extend` block joins an imported source, or whose file imports that base selectively. **What to do:** nothing. Queries that answered live now read the table; the rows are the same.

**[fix] A file is no longer warned about an unstored source it cannot name.** When an unstored source's join reads a stored source in another destination, the `cross_connection_join` warning was raised in every model that compiled the declaring file, including one that imports only a stored source beside it (`import { activity } from "activity.malloy"`). That warned about a source no query in that model can reach. The warning now appears only where some source a caller can name reaches the unstored one. **Who is affected:** authors reading these warnings in importing files. **What to do:** nothing.

## [Unreleased] — a dataset-scoped BigQuery account's stored tables serve queries that compare strings

**[fix] On BigQuery, a stored table now serves a query that groups, orders or filters by a string when the connection's account can read only its datasets.** 0.18.6 (#2049) taught a `storage=` build to read each dataset's own `INFORMATION_SCHEMA`, so a chain of `storage=` sources over a `.table()` source builds on an account granted only its dataset (dataset READER and jobUser, no project-level `bigquery.tables.list`). The serve side still read the project-wide region views, which such an account is denied, so it could not prove the source compares strings byte-exact: every query that grouped, ordered or filtered by a string answered live, with the served copy's decline "the result groups or compares a string a stored table does not compare as its source does: a query that reads a string under a collation". Each bind now reads the project-wide views first and, when they are refused the caller, each dataset's own catalog instead, provided every table the model's `.table()` sources read is known and they span at most 20 datasets. A `storage=` build now uses the same order, so an account that can read project-wide runs the same two queries per project and region as before. An `.sql()` source and a view are still proved only by the project-wide reads. A read that is denied or incomplete still answers live, and now logs one warning naming the connection, project, location (when the connection sets one), dataset and a bounded reason (`dataset_unread`, `project_unread`, …), never a driver's text. **Who is affected:** BigQuery connections whose account is scoped to datasets: their stored tables now answer the queries above, at one extra catalog query per dataset at each bind and build. **What to do:** nothing.

## [Unreleased] — clearer advice on two stored-source warnings

**[fix] A `#@ persist` source is no longer told to inline a join it cannot inline.** When a stored source's join reads another connection, its `served-copy-not-served` warning (`cross_connection_join`) told every source to "inline the join (inline=)", but only a `#(materialize)` source takes `inline=`. The warning now gives that advice to `#(materialize)` sources only; a `#@ persist` source is told to materialize the joined source into the same destination, or to build itself in its own database. **Who is affected:** authors reading this warning on a `#@ persist` source. **What to do:** nothing.

**[fix] A `storage=` downstream over an inline `extend` is told to name its base.** A `#@ persist` source written as `source: x is up extend { … } -> { … }` over a stored `up` is refused (`upstream_table_unusable`) because its query's base has no name to read its strings on. The message said only that "the base its strings are read on is not named". It now says the base is an inline `extend` or an unnamed query, and to declare that base as a source of its own and build this one over it by name. **Who is affected:** authors chaining `storage=` sources this way. **What to do:** declare the base as a named source (`source: up_with_users is up extend { … }`) and persist the query over it.

## [Unreleased] — the `malloy-pub` CLI publishes to npm as `@malloy-publisher/cli`

**[new] The Publisher CLI, `malloy-pub`, is now on npm as `@malloy-publisher/cli`, released in lockstep with the server.** Until now it was buildable only from a clone, under a package name (`@malloydata/publisher-cli`) that was never published, so the commands the materialization docs and skills show (`malloy-pub materialize`, `malloy-pub schedule set`, `malloy-pub list materialization` and the rest) had no install path outside the repo. Run it with `npx @malloy-publisher/cli@latest <command>`, or install the binary with `npm i -g @malloy-publisher/cli`. It needs Node.js 20 or newer and no Bun. Each release publishes it at the same version as `@malloy-publisher/server`, with its API client generated from that release's `api-doc.yaml`, so match the two when you pin; `malloy-pub --version` now reports that version rather than a fixed `0.0.50`. The commands themselves are unchanged. Nothing on npm ever carried the old name, so there is nothing to migrate from.

## [0.18.6] — a file kept from before a failed recompile no longer serves stale tables when its upstream read fails

**[fix] A stored table whose upstream could not be read no longer serves its last build while its file does not recompile.** Since 0.18.4, when a rebind could not recompile a model file that compiled before (most often a table it reads was dropped), the package kept the file's last good model and read its sources' upstream tables again, so the stored tables built from an upstream that changed answered live (`incompatible`, `upstream_altered`). When that read failed (a catalog query or connection error, a timeout), the failure counted as "unchanged": nothing was withdrawn, the stored tables kept answering from their last build even if their upstream had been dropped, their verdicts said `serves`, and the `model-recompile-failed` warning said nothing was withdrawn. A failed read now counts as unknown. Each stored table built from an upstream the read could not confirm answers live with the new serve verdict reason `upstream_unread`, and the warning and the stale message name the tables that could not be read. A failure that cannot tell which tables withdraws every stored table of the file. A failed reload or publish that keeps the previous package does the same. The withdrawal is held across plan refreshes (a connection edit's) until every file compiles again and the read succeeds, so a refresh cannot serve the tables in the meantime. They serve again once a read succeeds and finds the upstream unchanged. There is no server timer or backoff: the read happens only when the host's calls drive one, at the package's next manifest bind (a `storage=`-only package's included) or rebind (a run's commit, or a poll of an unchanged manifest, which no longer skips while one is withdrawn), or when a reload or publish plans the package afresh. **Who is affected:** packages with `#@ persist` or `#(materialize)` sources in a file that stopped recompiling while the upstream read also failed; their queries could return a stale answer. **What to do:** nothing. Clients that branch on a verdict's `reason` should expect `upstream_unread` (the set is open).

## [0.18.6] — render-tag package warnings carry a `code`

**[fix] Every render-tag finding on a package now carries a stable `code`.** A render annotation the renderer cannot apply as written (malformed for its field, or inert where it sits) used to appear in a package's `warnings` with no `code`, and a client that read `code` on every warning could fail on it. Each such warning now carries `code: "render-tag"`, the name a package-scope compile already gave these findings. A package-scope compile that could not finish a model's render-tag check (the model could not be read, or the validator failed) now reports that finding as `render-tag-check-failed` rather than `render-tag`, so a client can tell "unknown" from "a tag is wrong". **Who is affected:** clients that branch on a warning's or compile problem's `code`: expect these two values, and stop treating a missing `code` as a render-tag finding. The messages are unchanged and may still change; the codes are the stable part.

## [0.18.6] — stored sources read through a `.sql()` source's `%{}` serve, and no longer take their file down

**[fix] A `.sql()` source that reads a stored source through `%{}` no longer turns off serving for its whole file.** Take two `#@ persist` sources unioned in SQL: `source: outreach_daily is conn.sql("""select * from %{ email_daily_rows -> { select: * } } union all by name select * from %{ linkedin_daily_rows -> { select: * } }""")`. The served copy of that file did not compile ("No virtual-map entry for virtual source …"). Every stored source in it, and in every file importing it, then answered live with `compile_failed`, including sources no `%{}` reads. A bare `%{ x }` of a stored source did the same on any tier ("Source is not persistable, cannot be used in SQL"). The served copy now compiles with the tables it re-roots, so in the sources' own database the union is served from both tables. A source a `%{}` cannot read from its table is left as written, alone. That covers a source embedded bare, and one whose table is in a storage destination or a managed (DuckLake) catalog, which the `%{}`'s connection cannot reach. The file's other sources serve, and so do those of every file that imports it, even one that imports only some of its names.

**[fix] A stored source read only through a `.sql()` source's `%{}` no longer reads `unreachable`.** The reach walk follows each `%{}`, so such a source reads `serves`. The query's path report names each table the union's own `%{}` read as `used`, never a table read only through a join.

**[fix] Where a `%{}` cannot read a stored table, the verdict says why.** Such a source's verdict is `live` (`served_copy`) with a new `notServedIn` reason, and a `served-copy-not-served` warning names the `.sql()` source and its connection. `publisher_served_copy_bind_total` counts both new reasons.

- `sql_embed_cross_connection`: the `%{}`'s SQL runs on another connection than the table. Fixes: persist the `.sql()` source itself with the same `storage=` as what it reads, or drop `storage=` from what it reads. On a DuckLake or managed connection, build what it reads into a warehouse table read with `.table()`.
- `sql_embed_bare`: a bare `%{ x }`. Fix: write it as `%{ x -> { select: * } }`.

**[fix] A refused downstream's message no longer says it is answered "over" its upstream's table.** That was not true where the upstream's table is not served. The message now says only that it is answered live. 0.18 and earlier said this too.

**Who is affected:** a package with a `.sql()` source whose `%{}` reads a stored source. **What to do:** nothing in a source's own database with `%{ x -> { … } }`; otherwise, read the verdict's fix.

## [0.18.6] — a rollup checks the key of a `join_one` its grain reads

**[feature] A coarser query is served again once the joined key is proven unique.** A `#(rollup)` whose grain reads through a `join_one` (`grain=["account.region", "period_month"]`, or `region is account.region` in the grain) answered every query that read nothing through the join live, since a repeated `account_id` would have inflated the partials its build summed. Each build of such a rollup now also checks the join's key in the joined source, as a query of that source by name reads it (its own `where:` included), and records the verdict in the table's column contract. Unique, `run: subs -> { group_by: period_month; aggregate: mrr }` is served from the rollup again. Repeated or unchecked, it is still answered live (`COUNT_SEMANTICS`), and the detail says which; a repeated key also raises `rollup-join-one-key-repeated` on the rollup's source while that table is bound. A rebuild checks again. The `publisher_materialization_key_check_total` counter gains the kind `grain_join`. No API field is added.

## [0.18.6] — a same-catalog read reaches no further than the managed connection would

**[security] A served copy and a build that read a managed DuckLake connection's tables with a storage destination's credential hold those tables to the connection's own scope, and check it each time.** When a destination and a `managed` connection are one catalog, the same-catalog build, and a served copy serving a join across them, read the connection's tables through the destination's session, whose credential reaches the whole catalog. Two things the managed connection's scope would stop were not checked when read that way: a table replaced by a same-named view, whose body is not held to that scope (the served copy checked only when it compiled, the build never), and a base table holding data files a catalog writer registered from another schema's storage, which the connection's scoped storage secret would refuse and the destination's would read. Now every table read that way must be a base table made only of data and delete files under the storage prefixes the connection's storage secret was built with when it attached, matched byte for byte on `/`-terminated prefixes. A served copy checks before every query it answers, failing closed to a live answer, and reuses a verdict while the catalog's snapshot id is unchanged, so it adds one small catalog read per query. A build from a managed connection checks inside its own transaction and fails when the check does. A build from an unmanaged connection, which reads the whole catalog itself, is unchanged. **Who is affected:** a catalog whose writers (the host or orchestrator) replace tables with views or register files across schemas. A managed same-catalog source whose build reads such a table now fails its build and answers live. **What to do:** keep each table's files under its own schema's directory, and point a stored source at base tables.

## [0.18.5] — a `#(rollup)` grain can name a one-hop join path

**[feature] A rollup grain may name a field through one join.** `#(rollup) grain=["account.region", "period_month"]` used to fail the publish and the load with `rollup-unknown-grain` ("the grain names `account.region`, a path"); a model written that way now loads, and its rollup is built and served (#2048). The path may go through a `join_one` or a `join_many` of the source to a public dimension of the joined source; it is stored as `account__region`, the `inline=` naming, and a query that groups or filters by `account.region` is answered from the rollup. A grain dimension that is exactly such a path (`dimension: region is account.region`, matched on its compiled definition) now serves the path too, so `group_by: account.region` stops answering live as `GRAIN_TOO_COARSE` on existing models with no edit. Through a `join_many`, the rollup serves only a query that groups by the path, since groups for different values share base rows; a query that drops it or only filters on it is answered live. A query reading another field of the join, aggregating through it, or returning an annotated joined field as its own column is answered live with the codes it had. Multi-hop paths and truncations through a path stay refused, each with its own `rollup-unknown-grain` message. See [preaggregation.md](docs/preaggregation.md#rollup-materialization-v2-behind-publisher_materialize).

**[feature] A dimension that is exactly a join path reports the joined field's `#(doc)`.** With no `#(doc)` of its own, `dimension: region is account.region` now describes itself with `account.region`'s doc in `GET …/entities` (the new optional `EntityField.docInheritedFrom` names the path) and in `get_context` (`description_inherited_from`), so a source that flattens a shared dimension no longer has to copy the doc. A doc written on the dimension wins; an expression over the path inherits nothing.

**[fix] A rollup whose grain reads through a `join_one` no longer serves an inflated coarser answer.** A `#(rollup)` (or `#@ preaggregate`) rollup with a grain dimension read through a `join_one`, such as `dimension: region is account.region` in `grain=["region", "period_month"]`, was built over that join. When the data repeated the joined source's key (two `accounts` rows with one `account_id`), every partial counted the matching base rows once per match, and a coarser query that does not read the join, `group_by: period_month`, was served from those partials: 340 where live answers 220. Live joins only for a query that reads the join, so such a query is now answered live (`COUNT_SEMANTICS`, its detail naming the join), whatever the data holds; a query that reads the join (`group_by: region`, `where: account.region = 'EU'`) is still served, and equals live. Anyone with such a rollup was affected; queries that read nothing through the join will now answer live until a build-time key check (a follow-up) can prove the key unique.

## [0.18.5] — a load into an existing table of an encrypted catalog no longer crashes the admin server

**[fix] A merge or replace into a table that already exists no longer aborts the process when the catalog is encrypted.** Catalogs are encrypted by default. Load sessions turned on DuckDB's Parquet metadata cache, and DuckDB 1.5.5 fails the second read of an encrypted Parquet file it has cached. A merge or a keyed replace into an existing table reads its target more than once, even when it changes nothing, and so does a keyless replace too large to compare in one pass. The failure invalidated the database and took the whole admin server down with it. Load sessions no longer use that cache. On 0.18.0 through 0.18.4, such a load into an existing table of an encrypted catalog restarts the admin server, so anyone using admin loads should skip those versions.

## [0.18.5] — a `storage=` extend of an unpersisted query over a stored upstream builds

**[fix] A `storage=` source declared as an `extend` of a query that is not itself persisted, over an upstream stored in the same destination, builds again.** Take `#@ persist storage=… source: user_sessions is _sessionized extend { … }`, where `_sessionized` is an unpersisted query (`engaged_events -> { … } -> { … }`) over the stored `engaged_events`. Every run failed it with "'user_sessions' compares a string over its stored upstreams ('engaged_events') that the destination, byte-exact, would compare otherwise than its source does: its string reads were not recorded", whether or not its upstream was incremental, and it answered live. The plan took every `extend` for a copy of a stored source's table, which compares nothing, so it recorded no string reads, while the run built the source over the upstream's table as any chained build, and refused it for want of them. The plan now records them unless the source shares the build of a stored upstream it reads, the one case the run copies as a projection; the strings it compares are judged against the upstream's recorded contract as for any chained build. **Who is affected:** a package with that shape. The `-> { select: * } extend { … }` workaround is no longer needed. **What to do:** nothing; the next run builds it.

**[fix] A downstream of a `storage=` upstream that failed in the same run names that failure.** In a host-instructed run, a database-tier downstream reading a `storage=` upstream whose build failed earlier in the run (such as a table colocated on the destination's catalog) was refused as "the host supplied an upstream entry this build cannot use … supplied at the wrong tier", blaming the host. It now fails as "its persisted upstream '<name>' failed to build in this run: <its error>", as a downstream of any failed upstream does.

**[fix] A BigQuery `storage=` build whose catalog read proves nothing now says so.** A `storage=` build on BigQuery records its string columns compared `none` in its column contract whenever its catalog read (`INFORMATION_SCHEMA` and dataset reads in the connection's projects) fails or sees too little, and every `storage=` table built over it that groups or compares those strings is then refused as `upstream_table_unusable` ("… which its upstream's table records as compared unlike live"). That read failed silently. It now logs one warning per build, naming the source, the connection, the project, the location and, when it got that far, the dataset and table, with a bounded `reason` (`table_types_unread`, `project_unread`, `table_not_listed`, …). It never logs the driver's text. Behaviour is unchanged. **Who is affected:** an environment whose BigQuery connection cannot read its project's catalog, where downstreams are refused on every run, full rebuilds included. **What to do:** grant the connection's service account READER on the datasets the warning names (or, for author SQL and views, `bigquery.tables.list` on the project), then rebuild the upstream.

**[fix] A BigQuery `storage=` build reads the catalog of the datasets it reads, not the whole project's.** To record how its strings compare, a `storage=` build on BigQuery read the region's project-wide `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` (`COLUMNS`, `COLUMN_FIELD_PATHS`, `TABLES`), which needs the project's `bigquery.tables.list`. A service account granted READER on its datasets (with `jobUser` and `readSessionUser`) but not that permission was denied every read, so every string column was recorded compared `none`. Every chained `storage=` build over such a table that groups or compares a string was then refused as `upstream_table_unusable` ("… which its upstream's table records as compared unlike live"), on every run, full rebuilds included. A build whose source reads only `.table()` tables now reads each of those datasets' own `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` instead, one query per dataset for up to 20 datasets, which dataset READER covers. A build that reads author SQL (`.sql()`), whose tables are not known up front, one reading more than 20 datasets, and one reading a view still read the project-wide views. A denied dataset read still records `none`, and logs `reason` `dataset_unread`. **Who is affected:** a BigQuery connection whose service account holds dataset-level READER but not project-wide `tables.list`. **What to do:** nothing; the next build of the upstream records its contract and its downstreams build.

## [0.18.5] — a stored table joined across one catalog is served, and a `CROSS_CONNECTION` decline names the join

**[fix] A stored table joined to an unstored source on the same DuckLake catalog is served.** On a managed database the host configures each catalog twice, as a storage destination and as a `managed` DuckLake connection (both `credible` on Credible). A `#(materialize)` source on the connection, `kept_orders` with a `join_one: customer` to a source left on the connection, was served for plain queries, but `group_by: customer.customer_id` was answered live as `CROSS_CONNECTION`: its served copy read `kept_orders` from the destination and `customer` from the connection, and Malloy refuses a join across connections. When the two are one catalog, by the build's own check, the served copy now reads the connection's tables through the destination too, as the same-catalog build already does, and the join is served. It does so only when every table it moves passes the managed connection's scope check (its `main` and `readableSchemas`) and is a base table, not a view, and nothing it moves carries author SQL (an `.sql()` source or a `sql_*` expression). Otherwise the query is answered live, as before. Each moved source keeps its own `where:`, givens, `#(authorize)` and access filters as written, so the answer is live's. Rows were already equal; only the speed changes.

**[fix] A query answered live as `CROSS_CONNECTION` says which join and which connections.** When the served copy reads a stored table from its storage destination and a join of that source reads a source on another connection, the copy leaves the join out, and a query through it is answered live. The path report's detail said only "a join to a source on another connection". It now names the join, the source declaring it, and both sides: "The query uses the join \`wh_customer\` of \`wh_orders\` (connection 'wh' into storage destination 'lake'), …". The destination is named as configured, never by the alias the served copy reads it through.

**[fix] The cross-connection warning advises dropping `storage=` only where it was written.** The `served-copy-not-served` warning for such a join (reason `cross_connection_join`) ended by advising "build this source in its own database (drop \`storage=\`)". For a source the host placed in a destination, with no `storage=` in the model (an orchestrated package), there is nothing to drop, so that advice is left out; the others (inline the join, materialize the joined source into the same destination, store this source there) remain.

## [0.18.5] — a database `name=` in a dataset or schema that does not exist is refused at plan

**[api] New `RefusedSource.reason`: `container_not_found`.** A database `#@ persist`, `#(materialize)`, persisted view or query, or rollup whose `name=` places its table in a container its warehouse does not hold (`name="no_such_dataset.by_station"` on BigQuery) planned cleanly before, with no refusal and no warning, and every build then failed with "Not found: Dataset <project>:no_such_dataset was not found in location US". The plan now reads each target container once per connection and container (a BigQuery dataset's metadata in the project the `name=` names, else the connection's billing project (where the build's unqualified `CREATE TABLE` lands, which may differ from its configured default project), compared with the connection's location when it declares one; a Postgres, Snowflake or DuckDB schema), and refuses such a table as `container_not_found`, under its mechanism's `*-not-built` warning naming the container and the fix: create it, or change `name=`. A BigQuery dataset in another location than the connection's is refused the same way, naming both. A read that fails refuses nothing, and `storage=` tables are not checked. The build checks again before its first statement, so a container dropped since, or one the plan could not read, fails that source's build with a `container_not_found` error that `SourceFailure.retryable` reports `false`. **Who is affected:** a client that switches over `RefusedSource.reason` sees a new value; a package with such a `name=` now shows the source refused, answered live, rather than planned and failing every build. **What to do:** nothing, beyond handling the new value; create the container or fix the `name=` to build the table.

## [0.18.4] — a dropped upstream table no longer takes its whole model file down

**[fix] A file keeps serving when one of its upstream tables is dropped.** Take a model file with two persist sources, one built over a table that was later dropped. On 0.18.3 and earlier, a worker that bound again after the drop (a run's commit or a manifest bind) recompiled the file and failed to resolve the dropped table. It then replaced the file's model with its compile error, so every query on every source in the file answered 424 `Error(s) compiling model … Not found: Table`. Workers that had bound before the drop kept serving, and nothing in `/status` said why. Now a file that compiled before and fails to recompile on a bind keeps its last good model, as a failed package reload keeps the package, but only when neither the file's text nor that of any file it imports changed since that model compiled, so the failure came from outside the package. An author's edit that fails to compile is never kept: it answers with its compile error exactly as before, so a removed source stops answering, a broken report is listed with its error, and a gate tightened in the same failed edit is never bypassed by the older model. The sources whose upstream table changed stop serving their stored tables: they read `incompatible` with `upstream_altered` and answer live (for a dropped table that live query fails for that source alone). Sources whose tables are intact keep serving. A new package warning, `model-recompile-failed` (`reason` `compile_failed`), names the file, its sources, the compile error, and which sources answer live. The package also reads `stale: true` in `/status` `loadErrors` (and in `get_status`, `list_packages` and `get_context`'s note), with the same message. Both clear on the next bind or reload that compiles the file. A plan re-derived meanwhile (a connection edit, say) keeps the withdrawn sources answering live. A run is not refused, since the files are the kept model's. One known difference: a restart, or a fresh load, with the table still gone has no earlier model to keep, so the package fails to load as before (a load error naming the file), while a worker already serving it keeps the rest of the file serving. An upstream on DuckDB whose table is dropped is not detected as changed, because DuckDB's read of it fails rather than reporting it gone, so its stored table keeps serving.

## [0.18.4] — long BigQuery queries no longer time out at about 18 minutes

**[fix] A BigQuery query that runs longer than about 18 minutes no longer fails with "The operation timed out."** `@malloydata/db-bigquery` asks BigQuery to hold each results poll for up to 120 s, but builds its HTTP client with the SDK's default 60 s request timeout. Every held poll was cut, the driver's retry budget ran out at about 17m50s whatever the connection's `timeoutMs`, and the job kept running (and billing) until its `jobTimeoutMs`, so a build's `CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT` could create its table after the run had given up on it. Publisher now gives each BigQuery connection's client a 180 s request timeout. The driver still does not cancel a job on that error path; that fix is upstream. Run logs (`materialization.build.failed`, `materialization.run.finished`) now carry the runtime's own text for a timeout or abort as `detail` beside its bare `code` (`23`).

## [0.18.4] — Package entities list a record column's members, and every join says how many rows it meets

The package entities (`ModelEntities.fields`) walked a record or repeated-record column (a BigQuery RECORD, a DuckDB STRUCT or STRUCT[]) as if it were a join to a source of the same name. When the model also had a top-level source with that name, the column's members (`lines.sku`, `lines.qty`) were never listed, and the column's `join` named that unrelated source. A record column is now always `nested`, with no `sourceName`, and its members are always listed under dotted names.

The same walk keys a record column's entries in `ModelEntities.sources` (its givens and `#(authorize)` gates) under its dotted path. On `orders` with record columns `delivery`, `lines` and `tags`, the entries were keyed `delivery` and `tags`, with nothing for `lines`. They are now `orders.delivery`, `orders.lines` and `orders.tags`, the same key the column's fields carry. A reader that looked a record column's givens up by its bare name finds them under the dotted path.

`EntityJoin` gains an optional `relationship`: `one`, `many` or `cross`, from Malloy's compiled join. A record column is `one` and a repeated record or array column is `many`, the same as `join_one:` and `join_many:`. Grouping by a field reached through a `many` or `cross` join gives one group per joined row.

## [0.18.4] — a materialization refusal names the annotation it is about

**[fix] Three refusal messages name the annotation the author wrote.** Codes and reasons are unchanged; only the wording moved. A `#@ persist` on a source Malloy cannot materialize (`persist-not-materializable`) now suggests marking a table-shaped source `#(materialize)` instead, which stores a table-shaped source as well as a query-shaped one, when materialization v2 is on. A build instructed with no storage destination for a source that declares `storage=` named every source as declaring `#@ persist storage=…`; it now names `#(materialize)` and the author's source for a `#(materialize)` source, `#(rollup)` (or v1's `#@ preaggregate`) with the base and grain for a rollup, and the view or named query for a persisted one.

## [0.18.4] — a `#(materialize)` source over a measured base serves in the files that import it

**[fix] A `#(materialize)` source whose base declares measures, views or joins is served from its table in every file that imports it.** With `bikes.malloy` declaring `trips is <table> extend { measure: … }`, `materialize.malloy` importing it and declaring `#(materialize) source: trips_2015 is trips extend { where: … }`, and `ext.malloy` importing `materialize.malloy`, a query on `trips_2015` was served through `materialize.malloy` but answered live through `ext.malloy`, which warned `served-copy-not-served` (`fields_not_carried`). The served copy keeps the base's `extend` block by finding the base the declaration names, and it looked that name up in the importing file's namespace, where `trips` is not visible, since Malloy imports are not transitive. It now reads the name in the declaring file's own scope (its declarations and its imports) and takes the declaration from whichever of the package's models holds it. That also fixes a chain of such bases across files (`trips_2015 is trips_mid extend { … }`, with `trips_mid` declared over `trips` in a third file), which was answered live even in the declaring file. A name the declaring file does not bind to exactly one source, such as a base imported under another name, still answers live.

## [0.18.4] — a Snowflake `.sql()` source no longer fails its publish at random

**[fix] A Snowflake `.sql()` source reads its schema on one session.** A model with a Snowflake `.sql()` source could fail its publish, or a reload, with "Table 'TT…' does not exist or not authorized", and publish moments later. The connector reads such a source's schema by creating a session-scoped temporary view and then describing it, each statement on its own checkout from the connection's pool. Publisher's pool holds up to 20 sessions and hands out the one idle the longest, so once it held more than one idle session the describe ran on a session that never saw the view; the longer a server ran and the more concurrent work it had done, the more often that happened. Publisher now runs the whole schema read on one session it borrows for the purpose. The cause is in `@malloydata/db-snowflake`, and this is a mitigation until the connector pins the read itself.

## [0.18.4] — a source over a failed persisted upstream says why

**[fix] A persisted source whose persisted upstream failed to build names that upstream and its error.** When a `#@ persist` source failed to build, every persisted source reading it failed with Malloy's internal "Persisted source 'bad@fail.malloy' not found in manifest (buildId: …); strict manifest mode forbids fallback to live compilation." The run's failure reason for such a source now reads "Failed to materialize source 'bad_down': its persisted upstream 'bad' (fail.malloy) failed to build in this run: <its error>", and, when no build of the upstream failed in the run, that the upstream has no table the build can read. Malloy's note for a source split by givens, and a build manifest's load error, are kept. How the failure is classified for retry is unchanged.

## [0.18.4] — a `MISSING_FIELD` detail names only the queried source's columns

**[fix] The path report's `MISSING_FIELD` detail names only the columns the query reads.** A query naming a column a stored table leaves out of its type (`run: s_geo -> { select: start_station_id, v }`) is answered live, and `path.considered` says why. When other sources in the same model file also left out a column named `v`, each with its own types, the detail listed every one of them. It now names only the queried source's column and its joins', a joined source's by its join path (`column \`geo.v\``), and lists only those tables. Where the queried source cannot be told, it names every table as before.

## [0.18.3] — `storage=` tables with a geography or geometry column serve again

**[fix] A `storage=` table with a geography or geometry column no longer fails its own column contract.** On 0.18.0 to 0.18.2, any `storage=` table in a DuckLake destination holding a geography or geometry column with a coordinate reference system (a BigQuery `GEOGRAPHY`, a DuckDB `GEOMETRY('OGC:CRS84')`) was found `incompatible` (`column_retyped`) at every bind, right after its own build, so every query on it was answered live and every run rebuilt it. The build read the column's type inside its transaction, where it carries its CRS; DuckLake's catalog keeps no CRS, so every read after the commit says `GEOMETRY`. A contract now records and compares a GEOMETRY as committed, without its CRS. Existing tables serve again at their next bind, with no rebuild. The CRS changes no stored answer: the values are the same, and no stored query reads a geometry column, which Malloy types as `sql native`, so a query that reads one is still answered live. A host that records `builtFrom[].contractDigest` (Publisher's own runs do not) sees that digest change once for such a table, so a `storage=` table it stacks on one rebuilds once.

**[fix] The path report names a table its contract left out.** A query's `path.considered` reported a `storage=` table the bind left out against its column contract as `NOT_BUILT`. It now reads `NOT_SERVED` with `code` `incompatible` or `contract_missing`, with a warning that says so.

## [0.18.3] — colocated BigQuery tables compare strings from their tables again

**[fix] A colocated BigQuery table serves string comparisons again.** Since 0.18.0, every query that grouped, ordered, filtered or scoped by a string over a colocated BigQuery table (a `#@ persist`, `#(materialize)` or rollup table in the source's own BigQuery dataset) was answered live, refused as "unknown collation (a BigQuery table unmatched)". BigQuery's `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS` reports an uncollated column's `collation_name` as the string `'NULL'`, and a build recorded that in the table's column contract as a collation, `bigquery:NULL`, which matches no source's. A build now reads `'NULL'` (in any case, padded or not), the empty string and NULL as no collation (`binary`), by the same rule the serve side's catalog read uses, and a `bigquery:NULL` an earlier build recorded is read as `binary`. Existing tables serve again at their next bind, with no rebuild; none is found `collation_changed`. A host that records `builtFrom[].contractDigest` (Publisher's own runs do not) sees that digest change once for a table with an uncollated string column.

## [0.18.2] — a wide manifest bind no longer holds the main thread

**[fix] Binding a manifest with many `storage=` tables no longer stalls the server.** Since 0.17.3 a bind recorded every named source's scope facts for every bound table in one main-thread task. On a package with many sources and dozens of bound tables that held the event loop for seconds or longer, long enough for a health check to time out. The bind now walks each source once, reuses that walk for every bound table the source's scope does not read, and yields to the event loop as it goes. What a query reads is unchanged.

## [0.18.1]: a data app learns where each answer came from and the reader's light or dark mode

**[new] The browser runtime (`/sdk/publisher.js`) gives a data app what Publisher knows about its answers.**

- `Publisher.query(model, q, { meta })` and `queryFull` fill `meta` with `servedFrom`, `path` (the table that served the answer and the ones considered) and `executionTimeMs` from the response, and `versionId`, the version the query was pinned to or `null`. Without `meta` nothing changes.
- `Publisher.model(modelPath)` reads a model's sources and fields with their annotations, and `Publisher.packageResource("build-plan" | "materializations")` what Publisher builds for the package and its runs. Both read the page's pinned version, as its queries do; another resource name is refused.

**[new] Light and dark between a framing page and a data app.** The page hears the reader's mode as `publisher:color-scheme` (`{ type, mode }`), asks for it with `publisher:color-scheme-request`, and answers `publisher:color-scheme-applied` once it has drawn it. The runtime handles the page's side: `Publisher.colorScheme`, `Publisher.onColorScheme(fn)` and `Publisher.colorSchemeApplied(mode)`. The SDK's `DataAppViewer`, and so the console, sends the console's mode to the page's own origin and gives the frame the page's colour scheme once the page answers; it exports the three message names and `PublisherColorScheme`. `Publisher.embed` does not send a mode.

**[new] The `malloy-html-data-apps` skill builds from a kit.** An agent asked for a data app copies the kit and writes one config and its pages: several pages with drill-downs, every block explained on its back, nine themes, light and dark. A dashboard request goes to `malloy-reports` unless the user asks for an app.

## [0.18.1] — a framed data app can save files, copy, go full screen and open new tabs

The frame that the Console's data app viewer and `Publisher.embed` create now adds `allow-downloads allow-popups` to its sandbox and delegates `clipboard-write; fullscreen`, so a page can save a file, open a link in a new tab, copy text and go full screen. A tab it opens keeps the sandbox: in Firefox a tab that escaped it could redirect the host page. Hosts that call `Publisher.embed` get this on upgrade with no change of their own. A host that passes `allow` replaces the default, and `allow: ""` turns it off; `null` takes the default. A host that passes `sandbox` replaces the sandbox tokens, so `sandbox: "allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-forms"` keeps the old frame. With the defaults, top navigation and modal dialogs stay off.

## [0.18.1] — Value search: index a report-gated model locally by listing the reports you work on

**A source gated by `#(access_filter) report_id = $REPORT_ID` can now have its values indexed on a local server.** Until now any gated source was skipped, so on a per-report model like this, `dimensional_value` searches found nothing locally. List the reports to index in `publisher.config.json`:

```json
"retrieval": { "dimensionValues": { "givens": { "my-package": { "REPORT_ID": [123, 456] } } } }
```

Each `#(index)` dimension is read once per listed report, through its gate, and each value is stored with its report. A `get_context` call returns a value only when its `givens` name that report, as hosted Credible does. A source that filters on a given with a plain `where:` and no default is read with these givens too.

A source with an `#(authorize)` lock is read the same way, and at search time its lock is checked against the caller's `givens` with the same check a query runs, so a caller the lock refuses gets none of its values. A source is read once for each combination of listed givens it actually names, so a source that names none is read once.

With nothing listed, these sources are still skipped, and the server log now names the setting. Nothing reads every report at once: on a production model that scans the whole table, and the 5,000-value cap would leave almost every report with no values. The setting lives in the local server's config, so publishing a package never carries it. See "Dimension value search" in `docs/configuration.md`.

**A model edit no longer reads every value again.** Each read is now stored in `publisher.db`, per dimension and per listed report, and reused by later builds: after a model edit, a reload or a restart. A read is reused while it is less than 24 hours old, its source's compiled definition is unchanged, and its connections point where they did; a rotated password or token does not count. Docs and line positions don't count, so editing a doc reads nothing. Changing anything else in a source reads that source's `#(index)` dimensions again, and listing one more report reads only that report. Before, every save in watch mode read every dimension again: about a minute against Snowflake on a model with a few dozen dimensions.

**`--init` keeps the search index.** `--init` still resets environments, connections, packages and materialization records from `publisher.config.json`.
