Now every database table a build writes carries it, a table Publisher named and one a host's build instructions named included, and the mark gains where the table is: `… owner=<environment>/<package> table=<location>`, the table's fully qualified location as the warehouse's catalog reports it (`<database>.<schema>.<table>`, or `<schema>.<table>` on MySQL, each part URI-encoded, dots included, and the whole value encoded again in the mark, so a `%` reads `%25`), read by one probe right after the build. Where the location cannot be read, the mark names no place, as 0.15.0's did. A `storage=` table is not marked. The mark is written best-effort as before: a mark that cannot be written is logged and the build stands, and nothing about what is built or served changes. The new drop route accepts a mark only when it names the place the requested name resolves to now, since a comment travels with a renamed, moved or cloned table and a search path can find another schema's table first.

**Who could notice:** the mark **replaces any table comment (on BigQuery, the table's description; on SQL Server, its `MS_Description` property) you set on a materialized database table, on every build**, where before only `name=` tables were overwritten; keep your own notes elsewhere. Anything that reads table comments sees the mark on more tables, and each build issues up to two more statements (the catalog probe, and `COMMENT ON TABLE` or its dialect's equivalent, such as BigQuery's `ALTER TABLE … SET OPTIONS`). On BigQuery the probe is an `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` query, billed for each database-tier build at BigQuery's minimum bytes charge. The mark proves ownership to the drop only where whoever can edit a table's comment or description could also drop it (not so for BigQuery's `bigquery.tables.update` or Databricks' `MODIFY`): grant those edits accordingly.

**Downgrading to 0.15:** a 0.15 server reads every mark that names a table as no mark at all, so its ownership protection falls back to run records alone, as before marks existed: a `name=` build is allowed only where the package's own records name the table, and a reclaim, or a run delete followed by your own drop, has no mark to tell it that another package has since built a table its records name.

## [0.16.0] — (BREAKING) an incremental source with a date or timestamp watermark no longer skips rows that land late; without `merge_key=` a refresh replaces the range it re-reads, and `lookback=` re-reads a window

**Fixed: rows loaded after a refresh, but stamped before it, were never written.** A `#@ persist` or `#(materialize)` source with `refresh="incremental"` and a `date` or `timestamp` watermark started each delta at the previous refresh's START TIME. A row stamped before that run started but loaded after it (an ETL that stamps rows when they are extracted and lands them minutes later, say) was below every later delta's range, so no refresh ever wrote it, while the source reported its refreshes as deltas and kept serving the table: queries answered from it undercounted until a full rebuild. `merge_key=` did not help, since the range is applied before the merge. A delta now starts at the newest watermark the stored table holds (at or below the boundary the last refresh recorded), read with one `max()` over its watermark column, so a row stamped at or after the newest stored row is read however late it lands. The start is inclusive, and a merge or a range replace re-reads that instant without writing a row twice. A read of the newest stored row that fails rebuilds the source in full, as any other failed probe does. This changes what an existing refresh reads: each delta now re-reads from the newest stored row rather than from the last run's clock (on a `date` watermark, the newest stored day on every refresh). A `number` or `string` watermark's boundary was already the newest value the source held, and is unchanged. This applies to every run, a host's instructed runs included.

**Changed, and why this release is breaking: without `merge_key=`, a refresh now replaces the whole range it re-reads.** A range replace deletes its range and inserts what the source holds there, and that range now starts at the newest stored row (a whole day, for a `date` watermark). So a stored row the source no longer holds in that range is removed, as a window-replacing refresh removes it. **Who could notice:** a source that drops or trims recent rows, such as a staging table that keeps only the latest day. If you need append-only behaviour, declare a `merge_key=`: a merge updates and inserts, and never deletes.

**Who was affected by the skipped rows:** incremental sources with a `date` or `timestamp` watermark whose rows can arrive after the time they are stamped with. **How to tell:** compare the served table with the source: `count()` over the source live against the same query served from the table (or `SELECT count(*)` on each), over a range that ends before the last refresh started. A difference is rows this skipped. **Recover them** with one full rebuild (`malloy-pub materialize --reseed`, or `reseed` on the run or the source's build instruction). This fix stops new rows being skipped; it does not bring back rows already skipped.

**New: `lookback="2 days"` on `#@ persist` and `#(materialize)`.** A row stamped _below_ the newest stored row, and loaded after it, is still below where a delta starts. `lookback=` starts each delta that much further back, and the merge key matches the rows read again. It takes a positive whole number and one unit, `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days` or `weeks` (singular or plural), or one letter as `freshness.window=` does (`"36h"`, `"2d"`); there is no month or year. There is no lookback unless you declare one. It is valid only with a `date` or `timestamp` watermark and a `merge_key=`, and at most 365 days: anything else fails the publish and the load (`persist-invalid`, `materialize-invalid`), and on a persisted view or query, which takes no incremental key, `persist-view-invalid` or `persist-query-invalid`. A 0.15 server does not know the key and fails the load of a package that declares it.

**New: rows a delta never reads are reported.** After each delta, one check counts the source's rows in the window just below where the delta started (as wide as the delta's own range, capped at seven days or the source's `lookback=`, whichever is longer) that the stored table lacks: with `merge_key=`, by keys and watermark, so a skipped restatement counts too; without one, the source's rows in the window less the table's. Any it finds are on the manifest entry as `lateRows` (`count`, and the window's `from` and `to`), logged at `warn`, and raised on the package as a warning, code `persist-incremental-late-rows`, while that manifest is bound. Both stay, with later findings added, until the source is rebuilt in full; the count is a lower bound, since each stretch of the source is checked once. The check is one aggregate per delta, gives up after 60 seconds (stopping its statement), and never fails a run; it is not run for a pair table, a string watermark, or a `storage=` source on BigQuery. A source whose watermark is a zoned timestamp (Postgres `timestamptz`, DuckDB `TIMESTAMPTZ`) on a connection whose setupSQL sets a session time zone other than UTC still rebuilds in full on every refresh, as in 0.15.0, and that is now logged at `warn` with the reason; a plain `timestamp` or `date` watermark is not affected. See [Incremental refresh](docs/materialization.md#incremental-refresh).

## [0.16.0] — security fix: a gate over a dimension computed from a string skipped the collation check

**Fixed: a stored table could answer a gated caller with rows live would not, when the gate read a dimension computed from a string.** 0.15.0 answers a gated or scoped query from a stored table only when every string comparison the gate makes compares the same way on the table as at the source, and skips that check when the gate compares no string at all. A gate (`#(access_filter)`) or a re-applied `where:` over a boolean or numeric dimension computed from a string column (an ordering, an equality, a `pick` or a function over the string) was read as comparing no string, so the check was skipped. Where that dimension is computed when the stored table is read (declared on a `#@ persist` source or any source extending one, or on a source extending a `#(materialize)` source), and the source column or the stored one compares strings under a case-insensitive or non-deterministic collation, the answer from the table could include rows live hides from that caller, or leave out rows live returns. Such a dimension now counts as the string comparison it is: the collation check runs, reads the collation of every column the dimension is computed from (through nested dimensions, renames and joins), and the query answers live unless both sides are known to compare alike. Where those columns cannot be named, as for a dimension read through a composite source or a computed stage output of a query-shaped source, a per-column dialect such as Postgres answers live. Gates over the string column itself were already checked and are unchanged. As with every gate, this holds only behind the gateway that sets the givens from a verified identity ([operating model](docs/security-posture.md#operating-model-a-microservice-behind-your-gateway)).

**Who was affected:** 0.15.0 packages that serve a stored table, in the database or in a `storage=` destination, past a row-level gate or under a re-applied `where:` that reads a boolean or computed dimension derived from a string column, where the source column, the stored table's column, or the instance compares strings under a case-insensitive or non-deterministic collation (a DuckDB `NOCASE` or `default_collation`, a MySQL `*_ci`, a SQL Server case-insensitive or a Postgres nondeterministic collation, and the like). Gates over numbers, dates, timestamps or the string column itself were not affected, nor was a dimension declared on a `#(materialize)` source itself, which its table stores as a column. Gates over computed non-string dimensions, such as truncations or arithmetic, may now answer live on Postgres when the database's default collation is not `C`, and a gate or scope over a computed stage output of a query-shaped source computed when a stored table is read (not one the source's own table stores), or over a composite source's dimension, now always answers live on Postgres. **How to tell:** such a query now answers live (`servedBy: "live"`) where 0.15.0 answered it from the stored table.

## [0.16.0] — security fix: a scope on a database table is judged by its source's collation

**Fixed: a `where:` over a database-tier stored table could admit rows live does not, after the table's column collation was changed.** A table a `#@ persist` or `#(materialize)` build wrote into the source's own warehouse holds the source's types, so an ungated `where:` (the source's own, an extension's, or a composite's) was re-applied to it without reading how the table compares strings now. An `ALTER` of a stored column's collation after the build changes no type, so it went unnoticed and the scope could return rows live excludes. Such a scope now reads the stored table's collation on every answer and answers live when it differs from the source's or cannot be read.

**Scopes keep serving while the stored column keeps its source's collation.** On Postgres, a database table is now judged against its source rather than an absolute bar: a scope is served when every column it reads (by any name it goes by: a rename, a flattened join, a dimension computed when the table is read) has the same resolved collation, library version included, stored as live. That holds for equality, ordering, `LIKE` patterns and string functions alike, under any default collation, a nondeterministic one included. A stage output read through an extension of a `#@ persist` source (`extend { where: … }` over it) is read as the stored column it is, not followed back through the stage. A caller's inline `extend` that adds no `where:` and no gate is judged as the source it extends. The same rule judges the columns a row-level gate reads on such a table. On Postgres a scope over a composite source answers live, since which member it reads depends on the whole query; a column given an explicit collation equal to the database default also answers live. DuckDB tables are judged by their definitions, as before. A scope the table does not compare as its source does is answered live, and the path report names the table as `NOT_SERVED` (a composite's member tables are not named there yet).

**Who was affected:** a scope (`where:`) on a database-tier persisted or materialized table whose stored column collation was changed after the build to one that compares differently. Tables left as built, and `storage=` tables (already checked), were not affected. **How to tell:** such a query now answers live (`servedBy: "live"`), with the table skipped as `NOT_SERVED` in its path report.

## [0.16.0] — new: drop a materialized table through Publisher, `DELETE …/connections/{connectionName}/materializedTables/{tableName}`

**New: a guarded drop of a materialization's database table** (`drop-materialized-table`). Deleting a run is record-only, and since 0.15.0 the raw SQL routes on `duckdb`, `ducklake` and `motherduck` connections run only a single `SELECT`, so a caller had no way to drop a table a run built there. `DELETE /api/v0/environments/{env}/packages/{pkg}/connections/{connectionName}/materializedTables/{tableName}` drops one database-tier table (the manifest's `physicalTableName`, URL-encoded) on a connection the package reaches, on every dialect, with the staging and backup copies a crashed build can leave when a terminal run record of the package still names the table on that connection (best-effort: a copy that cannot be dropped is logged and counted as a failed drop, and the answer is still 204). It takes an optional `materializationId` (the run that built it) and `versionId`, and answers 204. It refuses rather than guess, under the package's run lock and the table name's lock:

- 400 for a name the connection's dialect cannot quote, for a build's staging or backup copy of a table a run records (it is dropped with that table), or for a `materializationId` that is not one non-empty value;
- 404 for a connection the package does not reach, or a `materializationId` that is not a terminal run of the package;
- 409 `MATERIALIZATION_CONFLICT` while a run of the package is active;
- 409 `TABLE_IN_USE` (a new `Error.reason`) while a committed run of the package, of any version, other than the one `materializationId` names, names a table with this name in any place; while the run `materializationId` names is the one a version or the package serves; while a loaded copy of any package in the environment is bound to a table with this name; or when the warehouse refuses the drop because other objects depend on the table;
- 409 `TABLE_OWNED_ELSEWHERE` for another package's table, a view Publisher did not make, or a drop the warehouse refuses because the connection may not drop it or the name holds something other than a table; the answer does not name the holder;
- 409 `TABLE_OWNERSHIP_UNVERIFIED` when nothing proves it is this package's: no mark the route accepts, and the run `materializationId` names does not record the table on this connection, or the probe failed;
- 410 for an archived version.

A table already gone answers 204 while a run record of the package still names it there, and 404 `TABLE_NOT_FOUND` once none does. `TABLE_OWNED_ELSEWHERE` and `TABLE_OWNERSHIP_UNVERIFIED` still answer 400 on a build. Each drop counts on `publisher_materialization_drop_tables_total` with the new `occasion="caller"`; a refused drop is not counted. With the mark (see the ownership-mark section above), the record and the drop can go in either order, but drop first if you also want a crashed build's staging and backup copies cleared: they are dropped only while a run record still names the table. **A table built by an earlier release carries no mark the drop accepts until it is rebuilt:** drop it first, passing `materializationId`, then delete its run's record. Publisher does not authenticate the caller: restrict the route at your gateway to the operator that owns the package's materialization lifecycle, as you restrict the materialization routes. See [the drop route](docs/materialization.md#the-drop-route).

## [0.16.0] — a gated database `#@ persist` over a column its own query computes serves from its table again

**Fixed: a regression from 0.14.0.** A database `#@ persist` source with its own row filter (`#(access_filter)`) over a column its own query stage computes (`tenant is concat(category, '-x')`, filtered by `tenant in $GROUPS`) answered every query live in 0.15.0, where 0.14.0 served it from its table. The collation check added in 0.15.0 followed that column back through the stage to the string it is computed from, and read `concat` as a comparison other than equality, so it required a byte-exact (`C`) collation, which a Postgres database rarely has. The stage ran when the table was built, in the source's own warehouse as live runs it, so the stored column is what the filter compares, and it compares by equality: such a source is served again, with its filter grafted and proven as before, whenever the stored column's collation is deterministic. A stored column with a case-insensitive or nondeterministic collation still answers live, as does a stage computed when the table is read (a query-shaped source over a stored one). The path report also names that decline now: a query the served copy could not answer for its gate lists the source's own table as skipped with `ROW_LEVEL_GATE`, where 0.15.0 left `considered` empty with no warning. As with every gate, this holds only behind the gateway that sets the givens from a verified identity ([operating model](docs/security-posture.md#operating-model-a-microservice-behind-your-gateway)).

**Who was affected:** 0.15.0 packages with a database-tier `#@ persist` source that declares its own `#(access_filter)` over a column computed in its own query (a function, a `pick`, arithmetic over a string, and the like), on Postgres with a non-`C` default collation (`en_US.UTF-8` and most others). A filter over a column the query only groups by or selects, and DuckDB, were not affected. The answers were correct, only slower and costlier: they read the base tables. **How to tell:** in 0.15.0 such a query's path report says `servedBy: { "kind": "live" }` with an empty `considered`, though the table is built and bound; from this release it says `servedBy: { "kind": "materialized", "tier": "database" }`.

## [0.16.0] — an `except:` on a `#(materialize)` source whose base declares measures is served from its table

**Fixed: 0.15.0's `except:` fix covered only a base with no measures.** 0.15.0 serves a `#(materialize)` source with an `except:` from its table, but only when everything the source reads is stored in it. A base that declares its own measures, views or joins (`orders_raw is <connection>.table(…) extend { measure: revenue is amount.sum() }`, then `no_region is orders_raw extend { except: region }`) still answered every query live. A `served-copy-not-served` warning gave the reason `fields_not_carried`. The served copy keeps a base's measures, views and joins by writing the base's `extend` block again over the stored table, but it found the base from the compiled model. The compiled model records no base for an extension of a table-backed source, and Publisher's inference of one requires the extension to hold every field of its base, which an `except:` breaks. The served copy now also takes the base that the source's declaration names in its text, in the same file or a file it imports whole. That base must be a source on the same table that holds every field the source inherits. The step is then confirmed against the text, as every kept base is. The source is served from its table, its answers equal live, and the excluded column stays out of reach. If the kept block does not compile over the stored columns (for example, a base measure filtered on the excluded column, `measure: east_revenue is revenue { where: region = 'east' }` beside `except: region`), only that source answers live, and the package's `served-copy-not-served` warnings name it with both reasons: `reroot_not_compiled` (the re-root with the kept block) and `fields_not_carried` (the re-root without it).

**Who was affected:** 0.15.0 packages with a `#(materialize)` source that writes `except:` over a base declared as `<connection>.table(…) extend { … }` with its own measures, views or joins, on any connection. A base with no measures, a base with measures and no `except:`, and an `except:` written on the base itself were already served. **How to tell:** in 0.15.0 such a source's queries answer live (`servedBy: { "kind": "live" }`, with a `NOT_SERVED` candidate), and the package carries `served-copy-not-served` with reason `fields_not_carried` for it. Both are gone from this release on.

## [0.16.0] — a `storage=` answer on a Postgres source gives an integer past 2^53 as live does: a JSON string

On 0.15.0, a query on a Postgres source answered from a `storage=` table (a `#(rollup)`, a `#(materialize)` or `#@ persist` served copy, or a persisted view) returned a `bigint` value past 2^53 as a JSON number, where live returns the same value as a JSON string: `9007199254740992` served against `"9007199254740992"` live. The digits matched, since live on Postgres rounds such a value through JSON ([known limitation 12](docs/materialization-v2-plan.md#known-limitations-to-revisit)), but a client that reads the type, or a strict generated client, saw two answers to one query. The stored column is now read with live's `bigint` type, and the answer is rounded as live's is after the query runs, so a served answer equals live's in value and in type, sums included: a sum past 1e21, which live gives as a JSON number in exponent form (`1.8e+21`), is served the same way. A `bigint` column a `storage=` table holds as a float is left out and answered live, since its digits are lost. Database-tier tables are unchanged. Only Postgres is changed: the other dialects whose live answer rounds big integers (Trino, Presto, Databricks, SQL Server) are unmeasured and keep 0.15.0's behaviour. **How to tell:** on 0.15.0, a `bigint` field past 2^53 in a served answer (`servedFrom: "storage"`) on a Postgres source is a number rather than a string.

## [0.16.0] — new: the admin listener's request timeout is a setting, `PUBLISHER_ADMIN_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`

**New: `admin.requestTimeoutMs`** (`PUBLISHER_ADMIN_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`, `--admin-request-timeout-ms`), how long the admin listener keeps a request, its headers and an idle keep-alive open before closing the connection. The default is `600000` (ten minutes), the timeout every listener had before, so nothing changes unless you set it. A table copy or file load through the admin API answers only when the table is written, so a copy that runs longer than ten minutes lost its connection with the table still being written; raise this above the caller's largest copy, and keep the caller's own timeout above it. It applies to the admin listener alone: the main API and MCP listeners keep ten minutes. See [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md).

## [0.16.0] — a served copy that fails to compile no longer logs an unhandled rejection

**Fixed: a failed compile of a source's served copy also surfaced as an unhandled promise rejection.** The query that needed the served copy saw the failure and answered as before, but a second, internal promise rejected with no handler, so the server's process backstop logged an `error` for it and counted it on `publisher_unhandled_rejection_total`; a host embedding the server without that backstop could crash on it. **How to tell:** on 0.15.0, an unhandled-rejection log line and counter increment beside a served-copy compile failure. Neither appears from this release on.

## [0.16.0] — corrections to the 0.15.0 notes

The 0.15.0 notes left out two API changes, overstated two others and understated one. The behaviour shipped in 0.15.0 and is unchanged; only the record is corrected, and `api-doc.yaml` now says the same where it describes these. Readers working through the 0.15.0 checklist should read these beside it.

- **`RefusedSource.reason` `rollup_name_collision` is no longer produced.** A rollup's generated name now digests its declaring source, so no two rollups share one. The value is retained in the spec for records an older server stored. Add it to the retained values you accept beside the renames in the 0.15.0 checklist.
- **Both `sqlTemporaryTable` routes can answer 403** (`STORAGE_ACCESS_DENIED` or `PATH_ACCESS_DENIED`), like the query route and raw `sqlQuery`, when an object store refuses the database's read.
- **A missing privilege (`42501`) is not always unclassified.** On Postgres its message says permission denied, so `SourceFailure.retryable` reads `false`, as it did in 0.14.0. A Snowflake `42501` stays unclassified.
- **`MATERIALIZATION_REFUSED` is not answered on any route.** The eligibility gate runs inside a materialization run, after `POST …/materializations` has answered 201, so a refusal is recorded on the run: `SourceFailure.refused` and `refusalReason`, the run's `metadata.refusedSources`, or its `error`. No 0.15.0 route answers a 422 with it.
- **A gated query source's join to an ungated source's rollup in a `storage=` destination is served from that rollup, not answered live.** The 0.15.0 section on gated entry points over ungated stored sources says it is answered live. It is served from the rollup when the query source is stored in the same destination (admitted past its own gate, or holding only ungated rows), the joined source is ungated, the gate reads only the query source's own plain columns, and those columns are stored exactly and compared as the source compares them. Otherwise it is answered live (`ROW_LEVEL_GATE`).

## [0.15.0] — (BREAKING) upgrading from 0.14: the checklist

This release is a breaking minor. Every item below is explained in full in its own section further down; this list is what to check, in the order to check it.

**Before you upgrade the server**

- **Regenerate strict clients from this release's `api-doc.yaml`.** New enum values arrive on responses: `servedFrom: "database"`, `ServeVerdict.verdict: "awaiting_build"`, new `origin` values (`materialize`, `view`, `query`, `rollup`), new `RefusedSource.reason` values, new `SkipReason` values (`ROW_LEVEL_GATE`, `READ_FAILED`, `NOT_SERVED`, `OPTED_OUT`, `SHAPE_MISMATCH`) and new `Error.reason` values. A generated client that validates enums (pydantic included) rejects a response carrying one it does not know. Upgrade clients first, then the server.
- **Accept both spellings of every renamed wire value for this release.** Each value 0.14.0 shipped and this release renames is retained in `api-doc.yaml` as "retained, no longer produced", and Publisher still reads it on records an older server stored. The renames, with their aliases:
  - tier `colocated` → `database`, everywhere a tier is named;
  - `origin` and `RefusedSource.tier` `preaggregate` → `rollup` (origin) and the rollup's real tier;
  - `RefusedSource.reason` `read_only_dialect` → `connection_cannot_hold_table`; `given_in_persisted_query`, `dynamic_projection`, `dynamic_join`, `dynamic_joined_where` → `reads_given`; `preaggregate_over_dynamic_source` → `reads_given`, `given_where_over_unstored_field` or `inherited_where_with_given`;
  - path report `SkipReason` `CONTRACT` → `ROW_LEVEL_GATE`, `RUN_FAILED` → `READ_FAILED`, `WARNED` → `NOT_SERVED`, and `WARNED` with `persist-opt-out` → `OPTED_OUT`; `QueryPathCandidate.code` `served-copy-not-served` → `served_copy`;
  - `ServeVerdict.verdict` `not_built` → `awaiting_build`; dry-run `cutoverPath`/`cutoverReason` → `servePath`/`servePathReason` (both emitted, old pair deprecated);
  - `manifestBindingStatus` `live_fallback` → `bind_failed`; run `metadata.trigger` `ON_DEMAND`/`SCHEDULER` → `on_demand`/`scheduler`;
  - package warnings `preaggregate-not-built` → `rollup-not-built`, `preaggregate-join-one-key-repeated` → `rollup-join-one-key-repeated`, `stored-native-schema-missing` → `database-native-type-missing` (each emitted under both codes for this release only);
  - load-failure codes `preaggregate-*` → `rollup-*`.
- **Stop relying on removed values.** No longer produced, with no replacement under the same name: the `persist-source-refused` warning; the eight per-cause rollup warnings `preaggregate-hidden-field`, `preaggregate-access-filter`, `preaggregate-time-zone`, `preaggregate-current-time`, `preaggregate-reads-given`, `preaggregate-unreadable-measure`, `preaggregate-join-level` and `preaggregate-name-clash` (each is now `rollup-not-built`, with its cause in `reason`); the `range_not_found` served-copy reason (now `definition_not_parsed`). Removed outright: the `dropTables` parameter on `DELETE …/materializations/{id}` (`true` answers 400), its SDK, CLI (`--drop-tables`) and Console forms, and the `realization=` key on `#@ persist`.
- **Change dashboards and alerts on these metric labels**, which no alias can carry. A panel on an old label sees no new series after the upgrade; change it, or span both with a regex on the value:
  - `publisher_materialization_build_total`, `…_build_duration_ms`, `…_build_read_bytes`: `tier` value `colocated` → `database`;
  - `publisher_materialization_stale_upstream_entry_total`: label `build` → `tier`, value `colocated` → `database`;
  - `publisher_materialization_drop_tables_total`: label `engine` (`in_warehouse` \| `storage`) → `tier` (`database` \| `storage`), plus a new `occasion` label;
  - `publisher_annotation_findings_total`: label `tier` (`malformed` \| `unservable`) → `outcome` (`invalid` \| `not_built`);
  - `publisher_query_route_total{reason}`: `CONTRACT`, `RUN_FAILED`, `WARNED` → `ROW_LEVEL_GATE`, `READ_FAILED`, `NOT_SERVED`, plus `OPTED_OUT` and `SHAPE_MISMATCH`; `{leg}` and `publisher_query_route_duration_ms{leg}`: `served` → `materialized`;
  - `publisher_materialization_build_total{kind}` and `…_build_duration_ms{kind}` gain `query`; `publisher_materialization_run_duration_ms` gains `outcome`;
  - `publisher_materialization_eligibility_refused_total` drops (each refusal now counts once per plan derivation): re-baseline it.
- **Update log queries** for the renamed materialization log fields: `materializationId` → `runId`, `destination` and `storageDestinationName` → `destinationName`.

**In your models**

- **Rename `#(preaggregate)` to `#(rollup)`.** 0.14.0 spelled the v2 rollup annotation `#(preaggregate)`; it still works for this release, with a `deprecated-preaggregate-annotation` warning, and a measure or source that carries both fails the load. On a rollup, replace `namespace="x"` with `name="x.<table>"` (`deprecated-rollup-namespace` warns until you do).
- **Fix what now fails the load.** A package that loaded on 0.14.0 fails to publish and load here if it has: `realization=` on `#@ persist` (remove it); a `name=` in a `scope: "version"` package whose table part the readable name would rewrite (a space, punctuation, a leading digit, `__`); a malformed `freshness.window` or `freshness.fallback` value; or, with materialization off, an invalid `#@ persist` line on a view. Run `compile_model` at scope `"package"` (or `POST …/compile`) before upgrading: it now reports what the load will refuse, except an unquoted or unsafe `#@ persist name=`, which only the load reads.
- **Expect some tables to be built, renamed or rebuilt once** on the first run after the upgrade, without any change of yours: a gated base's rollups (database and `storage=`) now build and serve, holding every caller's groups; a persisted named query's table drops its `_query` suffix; a cross-file `#(materialize)` extension and a same-SQL `storage=` twin move to a new address; a `#(rollup)` over a base with a dotted database `name=` moves into that container; a standalone table past its declared freshness window rebuilds, and so does every windowed table built before this release (its entry has no `dataAsOf`), once; a Postgres `storage=` table with an unconstrained `numeric` is stored as `DECIMAL` on its next full build.
- **A declared freshness window now applies on a standalone server.** Past its window a table answers live (or stale, with `stale_ok`) until a run rebuilds it.
- **Grant access to the container a gated base's rollups land in.** Those rollups now build every tenant's aggregates, ungated, into the rollup's or its base's `name=` container (or the connection's default schema), which may be more open than the base table; grant access to it accordingly, or give the rollup a `name=` in a container you control. A `storage=` one holds them in the destination.

**In your deployment**

- **DuckDB is locked down** (see its section). Before upgrading, find models and raw SQL that read remote files (`https://`, `s3://`, `gs://`) through a plain `duckdb` connection, read paths outside the package or environment directory (absolute paths outside it, `..`, symlinks, a top-level glob such as `'*.csv'`; relative and absolute reads of the package's own files still work), rely on `INSTALL` or extension autoload, manage secrets in SQL, or send raw SQL to a DuckDB-backed connection that is not one SELECT (several statements, `COPY`, `CREATE`, `ATTACH`, `SET`, `EXPLAIN`, `PRAGMA`, `CALL`, a `PIVOT` with no `IN` list). A model whose `.sql()` source or raw SQL expression breaks the one-SELECT rule now fails to load. Each needs the migration its section names; MotherDuck is locked but untested.
- **Configuration names are deprecated, not removed.** Every setting takes the name derived from its key (`mcp.port` is `PUBLISHER_MCP_PORT` and `--mcp-port`); the old names still work and warn. Startup now fails when an old and a new name disagree, when a `retrieval` key has the wrong type, and when a secret in the file is anything but a single `${VAR}` reference. **On Kubernetes, set `enableServiceLinks: false`**: a Service named `publisher-mcp` injects `PUBLISHER_MCP_PORT` and stops startup. In the Docker image, re-enable the `.mcp.json` write with `-e PUBLISHER_MCP_CONFIG_FILE_ENABLED=true`; an empty `PUBLISHER_NO_MCP_CONFIG` no longer does, and `PUBLISHER_NO_MCP_CONFIG=0` or a `SERVER_ROOT` other than `/publisher` fails startup.
- **Drop tables yourself after deleting a run.** A materialization delete only removes the record.
- **Servers that share a warehouse now drop each other's renamed tables.** Two servers serving the same environment, package, model and source against one warehouse (blue/green, or dev beside prod) reclaim each other's renamed tables after a `name=` edit. Keep them on separate schemas or destinations, or change `name=` on both together.

**If you run Credible's control plane (or another host) against this server**

- Accept `servedFrom: "database"` on query results (Credible's `QueryResult` and `DataManagementQueryResult` validators reject it until regenerated), and a `tier` field on `path.servedBy`.
- Read the `awaiting_build` serve verdict where `not_built` was, and `bind_failed` where `manifestBindingStatus` said `live_fallback`.
- Key on `Error.reason` instead of message text: `ACCESS_DENIED` (every gate 403), `STORAGE_ACCESS_DENIED` and `PATH_ACCESS_DENIED` (an object store's refusal, now 403), `BUILD_INSTRUCTIONS_INVALID` (400) and `MATERIALIZATION_CONFLICT` (409) on `POST …/materializations`, `MATERIALIZATION_REFUSED` (422), and `TABLE_OWNED_ELSEWHERE` / `TABLE_OWNERSHIP_UNVERIFIED` (400).
- Sync the `RefusedSource.reason` enum (now one record for every declaration not built, `reads_given` the one given reason) and read a rollup's refusal by `origin: rollup`, not `tier: preaggregate`.
- A run in which every source failed or was refused records a manifest of `failures` and no `entries`; key success on `status`, not on a manifest being present.
- A package whose every declaration is refused has a build plan with empty `sources` and populated `refusedSources`, not `null`, and a run with empty `buildInstructions` for it starts and builds nothing instead of answering 400.
- A BigQuery table with no dataset-qualified `name=` is refused at plan (`needs_qualified_name`) even when the host would supply a dataset of its own; the check reads the author's `name=` only.
- `SourceFailure.retryable` is now `false` (where it was absent) for a warehouse's own data or syntax error: SQLSTATE class 22 or 42 on Postgres and Snowflake, BigQuery `invalidQuery` or `invalid`. A retry fails the same way until the model or data changes; hold such builds rather than rescheduling them. Missing tables, columns and privileges stay unclassified.
- A gated entry point over an ungated `storage=` table is now served from it, so its serve verdict reads `serves` where it read `NOT_SERVED` `row_level_gate`.
- A version the host has bound or built serves live once its manifest is cleared, through reloads and restarts, and refuses a local run without `buildInstructions` with 409.

## [0.15.0] — (BREAKING) one vocabulary: `database` replaces `colocated`, `#(rollup)` replaces `#(preaggregate)`, and every reason has one name

**What changed.** Every value that named the wrong thing, or two things at once, has one name now. Each value 0.14.0 shipped is renamed with a retained alias: it stays in `api-doc.yaml` as "retained, no longer produced", Publisher still reads it on any record a client sends back or an older server stored (a manifest, a run record), and a client should accept both spellings for this release. A renamed package warning is emitted under both codes, with the same message, for this release only (the Console and the MCP tools show it once). A strict client regenerates from `api-doc.yaml` for the new values and fields.

**[C]** marks a value Credible's control plane or MCP tool reads.

**The tier: `database`, not `colocated`.** A table built in the source's own connection was `colocated` on some surfaces and `database` on others (`servedFrom`, `path.servedBy.tier`). It is `database` everywhere now; `colocated` is retained where it was an API enum value.

| Surface                                                                                                     | 0.14.0                                     | Now                                                                                                                 |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ServeVerdict.tier` (package read, `serveVerdicts`)                                                         | `colocated` \| `storage`                   | `database` \| `storage`                                                                                             |
| `RefusedSource.tier` (`buildPlan.refusedSources`)                                                           | `storage` \| `colocated` \| `preaggregate` | `storage` \| `database` (`colocated` and `preaggregate` retained); read `origin: rollup` to tell a rollup's refusal |
| Metric label `tier` on `publisher_materialization_build_total`, `…_build_duration_ms`, `…_build_read_bytes` | `colocated` \| `storage`                   | `database` \| `storage`                                                                                             |
| Metric `publisher_materialization_stale_upstream_entry_total`                                               | label `build` = `colocated` \| `storage`   | label `tier` = `database` \| `storage`                                                                              |
| Log field `build` on the line logged when a build recomputes an upstream from raw                           | `colocated`                                | `database`                                                                                                          |

**The annotation: `#(rollup)`, not `#(preaggregate)`.** `#(rollup)` is the rollup annotation, with the keys and meaning `#(preaggregate)` had. `#(preaggregate)` is read exactly the same for one release, with a `deprecated-preaggregate-annotation` warning per measure naming the spelling it found. A measure or source that carries both fails the load (`rollup-invalid`). v1's `#@ preaggregate` is unchanged. `PersistSourcePlan.preaggregate` keeps its name until `/api/v1`.

**`origin` names the mechanism on every surface that reports a table:** `persist` (`#@ persist` on a source), `materialize` (`#(materialize)`), `view` (`#@ persist` on a view), `query` (`#@ persist` on a named query) or `rollup`. In 0.14.0 everything but a rollup said `persist`, and a rollup said `preaggregate`. This covers `ServeVerdict.origin`, `PersistSourcePlan.origin` (`buildPlan.sources`), `StorageServeBinding.origin`, `ManifestEntry.origin` (which still accepts `persist`, an absent value and `preaggregate`; Publisher reads only whether an entry is a rollup), and, new, `RefusedSource.origin` and the path report's `servedBy`, `considered[]` and `notConsidered[]`. A strict client adds the new values to the plan, binding and manifest enums, or reads an unknown one as an entry that is not a rollup.

**Every other rename:**

| Surface                                                                                | 0.14.0                                                                                                                                                                   | Now                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Old value                       | [C]           |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------- |
| `RefusedSource.reason`                                                                 | `read_only_dialect`                                                                                                                                                      | `connection_cannot_hold_table`, the serve verdict's word for the same case                                                                                                                                                          | retained                        | [C]           |
| `RefusedSource.reason`                                                                 | `given_in_persisted_query`, `dynamic_projection`, `dynamic_join`, `dynamic_joined_where`                                                                                 | `reads_given` (below)                                                                                                                                                                                                               | retained                        | [C]           |
| `RefusedSource.reason`                                                                 | `preaggregate_over_dynamic_source` (rollups)                                                                                                                             | `reads_given`, `given_where_over_unstored_field` or `inherited_where_with_given` (below)                                                                                                                                            | retained                        | [C]           |

`ServeVerdict.reason` `rollup_over_stored_base` and the `preaggregate-over-stored-base` warning, which the docs listed and nothing produced, are removed from the docs.

**Dashboards:** a metric label cannot be aliased. A panel or alert on any metric row above sees no new series after the upgrade until it is changed to the new label and values (or spans both with a regex on the value, such as `tier=~"colocated|database"`).

**One given reason, on every mechanism.** Naming only: nothing is built or served differently.

- **`reads_given`**: the build would read a given, so its table would hold one caller's rows. It is the reason on `#@ persist`, `#(materialize)`, rollups, persisted views and persisted queries alike, wherever the given sits: in a field the source declares, in a join's `on:` condition, or in a joined source that is not stored per caller. The message still names where (for example "the join 'g' has a given in its `on:` condition"). It replaces `given_in_persisted_query` and the three `dynamic_*` values, all four shipped in 0.14.0 and now retained, no longer produced.
- **`given_where_over_unstored_field`** (new): a given-reading `where:` of the declaration's own over a field its table does not store (a field the rollup's grain drops, or a `#(materialize)` field that is not a stored dimension). Its fix differs from `reads_given`'s: add the field to the grain, or write the term over a stored dimension.
- **`inherited_where_with_given`**: a given-reading term inherited from a base, now on every mechanism.
- **A rollup over a caller-scoped source** was refused as `preaggregate_over_dynamic_source` in 0.14.0. It now takes one of the three reasons above, as every other mechanism does for the same case, including for a base whose given has no default. `preaggregate_over_dynamic_source` is retained, no longer produced.

For the service team to sync: `refusedSources[].reason`, the `*-not-built` records, and the `reason` label of `publisher_materialization_eligibility_refused_total`.

**Gate refusals are named by the gate's kind.** `access_filter` when a row filter (`#(access_filter)`) refused it, `authorize` for a lock (`#(authorize)`) or a gate that cannot be read, on every mechanism. In 0.14.0 a `#@ persist` source said `authorize` for every gate, so a client keyed on `authorize` for a row-filtered `#@ persist` source sees `access_filter` now.

**New fields, so no client parses prose for a cause:**

- `Package.warnings[].reason`: the bounded cause of a materialization warning. The refusal record's `reason` on a `*-not-built` warning, the served copy's reason on `served-copy-not-served`, the unread reason on `database-table-unread`, the kept table's reason on `table-kept`, the serve verdict's reason on a `materialization-*` verdict warning, and `storage_mode` on `materialization-storage-mode`. An open string.
- `ServerStatus.loadErrors[].codes`: the codes of a load failure's `[code]` lines, in order, each once.
- `SourceFailure.refusalReason` (the `RefusedSource.reason` of a refused source) and `SourceFailure.code` (`table-owned-elsewhere` or `table-ownership-unverified`).
- `Error.reason` on answers that had none: `ACCESS_DENIED` on every gate 403 (a gate that could not be decided answers the same; only the metrics and the log tell it apart); `MATERIALIZATION_REFUSED`, with `Error.refusalReason`, on the 422 a materialization refusal answers; `TABLE_OWNED_ELSEWHERE` or `TABLE_OWNERSHIP_UNVERIFIED` on the table-ownership 400; and `STORAGE_ACCESS_DENIED` or `PATH_ACCESS_DENIED` on a storage refusal (see the storage-refusal section).
- `Error.reason` on `POST …/materializations` refusals: `BUILD_INSTRUCTIONS_INVALID` (400) on every deterministic build-instruction or body refusal (a field of the wrong shape, an unknown `sourceEntityId`, `realization=SNAPSHOT`, one table named twice across a version's `buildInstructions`, a duplicated or mismatched ledger entry, an unusable `physicalTableName`), the message still naming the case; and `MATERIALIZATION_CONFLICT` (409). Two of its cases clear on their own, so a host retries later: a run already active, and a table another run is writing. Two do not clear until something changes, so a retry fails the same way: an auto-run of a package or version a host manifest serves, and a run of a non-latest version touching the tables a `scope: package` package's versions share. The message says which. `BUILD_PLAN_UNAVAILABLE` and `VERSION_NOT_LATEST` are unchanged.
- New package warnings for gate findings that only reached the server log: `row-level-gate-unexpressible` (an entry point inherits a gate whose field it no longer carries, so it denies every request), `row-level-gate-reads-no-given` (a gate that reads no given) and `row-level-gate-negated-membership` (a gate that negates a membership test, which an empty given turns into match-all, or one too deep to check). Each is `warn`; the model still loads. A deliberate deny-all lock, `#(authorize) false`, no longer counts as reading no given: it raises no warning, and no longer counts `cause="source_line_gate_no_given_reference"` on `publisher_authorize_row_level_rejected_total`.

**Documented:** the serve verdict's `stale` reason; every `QueryPathWarning.code`; `materialization-unreachable`, `materialization-destination-missing`, `materialization-connection-cannot-hold-table`, `materialize-pair-full-refresh`, `served-copy-not-served` and the `annotation-*` codes in the warning catalogue; `servePathReason`'s `inherited_gate` and `through_base`; `time_zone` on `#(materialize)`; `env_reference` and `empty_storage` as the plan's backstop behind the load's own `persist-invalid` refusal (no served package reports them).

**Fixed: a refused `storage=` rollup's serve verdict said `tier: colocated`.** It now gives the tier its own `storage=` puts it in, as its refusal record does.

**Fixed: a persisted named query's own skips read as `MISSING_FIELD`.** The query leg explained only the view leg's declines, so a skip in its own codes fell to the unexplained default in the path report and `publisher_query_route_total`. It explains both now.

**Unchanged, until `/api/v1`:** the run statuses (`MANIFEST_ROWS_READY`, `MANIFEST_FILE_READY`), `PersistSourcePlan.preaggregate`, `QueryPathServer.via: served_copy` and the `publisher_served_copy_bind_total` metric name.

## [0.15.0] — (BREAKING) every materialization declaration Publisher does not build is one refusal record

Every valid materialization declaration Publisher does not build is now one record in the build plan's `refusedSources`, with a bounded `RefusedSource.reason` and an `origin`, whatever its mechanism: `#@ persist`, `#(materialize)`, a persisted view or named query, and a rollup (`#(rollup)` or `#@ preaggregate`). In 0.14.0 only a `#@ persist` source a compile-time gate refused (and a rollup the eligibility gate refused) had one; the rest were package warnings alone. Each is still answered live, the package still loads, and each still carries one `warn` package warning, under its mechanism's code: `persist-not-built`, `materialize-not-built`, `persist-view-not-built`, `persist-query-not-built` or `rollup-not-built` (with `preaggregate-not-built` repeated beside it for this release only).

- **What breaks: the eight per-cause rollup codes are folded into `rollup-not-built`.** `preaggregate-hidden-field`, `preaggregate-access-filter`, `preaggregate-time-zone`, `preaggregate-current-time`, `preaggregate-reads-given`, `preaggregate-unreadable-measure`, `preaggregate-join-level` and `preaggregate-name-clash` are no longer produced (retained in `api-doc.yaml`). Each is `rollup-not-built`, with its cause in `reason`. A client that keyed on one must key on `rollup-not-built` and read the reason from the warning or from `refusedSources`.
- **`persist-source-refused` is removed,** as 0.14.0 announced.
- **New `RefusedSource.reason` values:** `reads_given`, `given_where_over_unstored_field`, `incremental_unsupported`, `materialization_off`, `multi_line_annotation`, `build_name_collision`, `run_target_unsupported`, `nested_result`, `inherited_persist`, `inline_unsupported`, `no_stored_columns`, `needs_qualified_name`, `generated_build_failed`, `hidden_field`, `access_filter`, `time_zone`, `unreadable_measure`, `unreadable_grain`, `join_not_in_grain`, `partial_name_collision` and `connection_cannot_hold_table`. `api-doc.yaml` says which mechanism raises each. `current_time`, `inherited_where_with_given` and `table_name_collision` are now raised by more mechanisms than `#@ persist`.
- **Keys.** A persisted view or query is keyed by the build source it would have had (`<source>__<view>__view@…`, `<query>__query@…`), a `#(materialize)` source by its own sourceID, and a rollup measure refused before its rollup is planned by its path, grain and destination, `<base>.<measure>[<grain>]@<model>.preaggregate.malloy` or `<base>.<measure>[<grain> in <destination>]@…` (name `<base>.<measure>`), so two refused declarations on one measure are two records. A v1 `#@ preaggregate` refusal is keyed `<base>.<measure>@…`, and reported once, by the file that declares the source.
- **A plan where everything is refused is a plan.** Such a package now has a build plan with empty `sources` and populated `refusedSources`, where it had none (`null`). A run with empty `buildInstructions` for it now starts and builds nothing, where it answered 400.
- **Newly refused at plan, with no answer changed:** a nested persisted view in the database (`persist-view-not-built`, reason `nested_result`), whose table the view leg could never read; and a `storage=` rollup over a DuckDB source whose grain dimension is a BLOB, INTERVAL, MAP or JSON column (`rollup-not-built`, reason `unreadable_grain`), which no stored read declares. Both tables were built and never read; they are no longer built.
- **The serve verdicts list each refusal** (`live`, reason `refused`).

## [0.15.0] — (BREAKING) packages that loaded on 0.14.0 and now fail to load; one code per mistake

Every case below fails the publish and the load, with one line per mistake ending in its code. Fix the line it names. `compile_model` at scope `"package"` or `"file"` now reports these before you publish (see the compile section).

**Newly failing:**

- **`realization=` on `#@ persist` is retired.** Any value, `"COPY"` included, fails with `persist-retired-key` ("remove it: every table is built by CREATE TABLE AS SELECT"). Nothing read it. The build instruction's `realization` field stays on the wire but is optional, absent meaning `COPY`; `SNAPSHOT` is still refused. A manifest entry's `realization` is retained and is always `COPY`.
- **A `name=` the readable name would rewrite, in a version of a `scope: "version"` package.** There a `name=`'s table part starts the table's readable name (`name="analytics.summary_t"` builds `analytics.summary_t__v1_2_0__p<8 hex>`), and 0.14.0 sanitized it without notice (`name="My-Table"` built `my_table__…`). Lowercasing is now the only change: a table part with a space, punctuation such as `-`, a leading digit, or `__` fails with its route's code (`persist-invalid`, `materialize-invalid`, `persist-view-invalid`, `persist-query-invalid`). Write it with letters, digits and single underscores, starting with a letter. In an unversioned or `scope: "package"` package a `name=` is the table's exact name and is not checked this way.
- **A malformed freshness value.** On `#@ persist` (a source, a view or a named query) and `#(materialize)`, a `freshness.window` that is not a whole number and a unit (`s`, `m`, `h`, `d`, `w`; so `"1 day"`, `"1.5h"`, `"PT1H"` and `"24"` are refused) or a `freshness.fallback` other than `live`, `stale_ok` or `fail` fails with `persist-invalid` or `materialize-invalid`, where 0.14.0 dropped it silently. On a rollup the same values fail with `rollup-invalid`, an unknown key in the group with `rollup-unknown-key`, and measures of one rollup that declare different freshness with `rollup-invalid`.
- **An invalid `#@ persist` line on a view, with `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE=false`.** With the switch off the line was never read. It is now read in both modes, as a persisted query's already was, and fails with the code it fails with when the switch is on (`persist-view-invalid`, `persist-view-unparseable`, `persist-unknown-key`, `persist-retired-key`); a valid one warns `persist-view-not-built`, reason `materialization_off`.

**Same failure, new code** (sync these if you parse codes):

- An unknown `freshness.` key on `#(materialize)` (`freshness.windw=`): `materialize-unknown-key`, was `materialize-invalid`.
- A `#@ persist` line on a view or named query that does not parse: `persist-view-unparseable` or `persist-query-unparseable` (new codes), was `persist-view-invalid` or `persist-query-invalid`.
- An unsafe or unquoted `#@ persist name=` (`name=t`): one line per offending annotation, each ending `[persist-invalid]`, as a 400; was one uncoded compile error (a 424).
- `sharing=` and `schedule=` on `#(materialize)`: `materialize-retired-key`, was `materialize-unknown-key`.
- A named query with a lone `refresh="incremental"`: `persist-query-invalid`, was `persist-invalid` naming its generated `<query>__query` build source.

**A persisted named query reports as `query`, not `view`:** `publisher_materialization_build_total{kind}` and `…_build_duration_ms{kind}` gain the value `query`, and a persisted query's decline codes are `query_missing_field`, `query_not_built` and `query_stale`, where they were the view's `view_*`. `api-doc.yaml` documents the codes, and no longer says an unrecognized `#@ persist` key rides through.

## [0.15.0] — (BREAKING) every answer from a materialized table reports its tier: `servedFrom: "database"` and `path.servedBy.tier`

A query answered from a table in the source's own database now reports `servedFrom: "database"`, where it reported `null`. This covers a database `#@ persist` table Malloy substituted, a database `#(materialize)` table the served copy read, and a database rollup or persisted view or query. `storage` and `live_fallback` are unchanged, and `null` now means only that no materialized table answered. The path report's `servedBy` gains `tier` (`database` or `storage`) whenever a table answered. The access record's `servedFrom`, the workload log's `served_from` and the `malloy.model.query.served_from` attribute on `malloy_model_query_duration` carry the new value too.

- **Regenerate strict clients before upgrading.** A client generated from `api-doc.yaml` that validates enums rejects a response carrying the new value. This includes pydantic validators such as Credible's pycommon `QueryResult` and `DataManagementQueryResult`, and a closed `servedBy` schema rejects `tier`.
- **A client that treats any non-null `servedFrom` as a storage hit** now counts database hits as well. Compare against `"storage"` to count the `storage=` tier alone.
- **A dashboard that read database hits as live** sees them move from `null` to `database`, with no change in which table answered or what it returned.

## [0.15.0] — (BREAKING) security: every DuckDB instance is locked down, and raw SQL on DuckDB runs as a single SELECT

**Security fix.** Every DuckDB instance Publisher created ran with DuckDB's defaults. SQL that reached one, a raw `sqlQuery` (on the package `duckdb` sandbox too) or model text (`duckdb.sql(...)`, `duckdb.table(...)`), could read any local file the server process could read, use the host's ambient cloud credentials and its cloud metadata service, and load community extensions or write persistent secrets. Every instance now runs under a lockdown chosen by what it needs:

- **No network**: the package sandbox runs under Malloy's `securityPolicy: "sandboxed"`, confined to its package directory (relative and absolute reads of the package's own files, `.xlsx` included, keep working). An environment `duckdb` connection with only `setupSQL` is confined to its environment directory, then runs its `setupSQL`, then is locked.
- **Networked readers** (`ducklake` connections, storage destinations, `duckdb` connections with `attachedDatabases`, `motherduck`, build and load sessions): each does its own setup (its catalog, its scoped secret, its extensions), then is confined to exactly the paths that setup reads, with external access off and its configuration locked.

The lockdown is part of each instance's configuration identity, so a locked instance is never shared with a connection that needs a different setup or policy. A consequence: after an edit to a `ducklake` connection or to a `duckdb` connection's `attachedDatabases`, the first query on the new connection waits for the previous generation to drain (up to about 30 seconds) before it opens the database file afresh.

**Who was affected:** any deployment where people who should not have the server's own reach could run SQL or write models: callers of the query endpoints with raw SQL, and package authors. Deployments behind a gateway that admitted only trusted callers and packages were not exposed beyond what those already had.

**BREAKING**, each with its migration:

- **Remote reads through `duckdb`.** A model or query that reads a remote file (`https://`, `s3://`, `gs://`) through a plain `duckdb` connection, the package sandbox included, now fails. _Migrate:_ read it through a configured connection: a `duckdb` connection whose `attachedDatabases` holds a credential for the bucket, or a `ducklake` connection.
- **Paths outside the connection's roots.** A read or write outside the package directory (the sandbox), the environment directory (an environment `duckdb` connection) or the data path (a DuckLake catalog) fails, absolute paths and `..` included. _Migrate:_ move the file under the root, or reference it through a connection whose root holds it.
- **`setupSQL` confinement.** `setupSQL` on an environment `duckdb` connection with no `attachedDatabases` runs confined: no network, nothing outside the environment directory, no `INSTALL` and no extension beyond `json`, `icu`, `excel` and `ducklake`. _Migrate:_ keep what it reads under the environment directory, drop `INSTALL` lines, and attach remote data through `attachedDatabases`.
- **Symlinks and globs in the sandbox.** A file that is a symlink out of the package is refused, and so is a relative glob over the package's top level (`'*.csv'`). _Migrate:_ copy the data into the package, and glob a subdirectory (`'data/*.csv'`) or name the files.
- **Extension autoload.** Autoload is off on a locked connection: only the extensions its own setup loads, plus `json`, `icu`, `excel` and `ducklake`, are available. _Migrate:_ use a connection type that loads what you need (`attachedDatabases`, `ducklake`); there is no per-connection extension setting.
- **Refused statements.** On a locked connection, SQL cannot create, replace or drop a secret, call DuckDB's logging or profiling functions, or run SQL taken from text (`query()`, `query_table()`, `json_execute_serialized_sql`, `IMPORT DATABASE`). _Migrate:_ configure credentials as connection settings; none of these has a replacement through SQL.
- **Single-SELECT raw SQL.** Raw SQL sent through the connection SQL routes to a DuckDB-backed connection (the package sandbox, or an environment `duckdb`, `ducklake` or `motherduck` connection) runs only as one SELECT, CTEs included, with the same 400 a managed DuckLake connection answers. Several statements, or anything that is not a SELECT (`COPY`, `CREATE`, `INSERT`, `ATTACH`, `SET`), are refused, and so are some forms that read: `EXPLAIN`, `CALL`, `PRAGMA`, and a `PIVOT` with no `IN` list (a dynamic PIVOT). `SUMMARIZE`, `DESCRIBE`, `SHOW` and FROM-first queries still run. When a package loads, author SQL on any connection whose SQL dialect is DuckDB (the sandbox, an environment `duckdb`, `ducklake` or `motherduck` connection, a storage destination, and a `publisher` proxy connection to a remote DuckDB) is held to the same rule: a `.sql()` source must be one SELECT (a dynamic PIVOT is refused there too), and a raw SQL expression (`sql_number()` and its siblings) must read as one expression of one SELECT with each of its arguments as a value; a model that breaks either fails to load. _Migrate:_ send one SELECT per request; give a PIVOT an explicit `IN` list; build tables with `#@ persist` instead of `CREATE TABLE` through raw SQL; pass a value to a raw SQL expression as an argument, never inside a quoted fragment.
- **MotherDuck (untested).** MotherDuck connections are locked like the other networked readers, but have not been tested against MotherDuck with external access off. If the lock, or a catalog read after it, fails, the connection fails with an error naming MotherDuck and the step. _Migrate:_ none known; report the error if a MotherDuck connection stops serving.

**Known residual:** confining a connection to its data path is not org isolation inside one shared bucket. Isolating orgs that share a bucket requires credentials the host scopes per org; see [security-posture.md](docs/security-posture.md#known-gaps), gap 6, which also lists the other limits.

## [0.15.0] — (BREAKING) `dropTables` removed from the materialization delete; a delete is record-only

**What breaks: `DELETE …/materializations/{id}` no longer takes `dropTables`.** Deleting a materialization run removes its record and nothing else, every time: it never drops a table. Removed with it: the `dropTables` query parameter on the delete (on the `/environments/…` route and the legacy `/projects/…` route), the generated clients' `dropTables` argument (the TypeScript SDK's and CLI's `deleteMaterialization` lose their fourth parameter, and the Python client is generated from the same spec), the "Also drop the materialized tables this run produced" checkbox in the Console's delete dialog, and the `malloy-pub delete materialization --drop-tables` flag.

**`dropTables=true` is refused with 400; `false` is accepted and ignored.** `?dropTables=true` answers 400 naming the parameter and saying that a delete is record-only, and deletes nothing; a 204 would read as the tables having gone too. `?dropTables=false`, which older `malloy-pub` releases and Consoles send on every delete, asks for exactly what a delete now does, so it deletes the record and answers 204. Any other value (`1`, `yes`) is refused with a 400 whose fix is to omit the parameter. A `malloy-pub` that still passes `--drop-tables` fails with an unknown option.

**Why.** A delete that also dropped tables had to decide, from the records alone, whether a table it was about to drop was still served by another run, another package or another name for the same place, and every guard added to that decision was another way to get it wrong on a customer's data. Credible's hosted control plane never used it; it drops tables through connection SQL. Publisher's own reclaims, which drop only what they can prove is theirs, are unchanged (see the rename-rule section).

**What to do instead.** Delete the run, then drop the table yourself through its connection: read the run's manifest for each entry's `physicalTableName`, `connectionName` and `storageDestinationName`, check that no remaining `MANIFEST_FILE_READY` run, of any version, names a table with that name in any place (list the runs of each published version with `?versionId=`, since the runs list answers for the latest version only; an auto-run carries unchanged tables forward under the same name, so an old run's table is often still served, and two destination names can reach one DuckLake), then `DROP TABLE` in the warehouse, or, for a storage destination, use the admin API's table delete. See [Dropping a run's tables](docs/materialization.md#dropping-a-runs-tables).

## [0.15.0] — (BREAKING) settings take their derived names; the old names are deprecated, and a conflict between them fails startup

Every setting now has one name of each kind, derived from its key: a variable (`PUBLISHER_` plus the key in upper snake case), a flag (`--` plus the key in kebab case, `--no-` for a boolean) and its key in `publisher.config.json`. So `mcp.port` is `PUBLISHER_MCP_PORT`, `--mcp-port` and `{ "mcp": { "port": 4040 } }`. `docs/configuration.md` lists every setting's names, generated from the registry. To write a `publisher.config.json`, start from [`publisher.config.json.example`](publisher.config.json.example) at the repo root: it holds every setting the file can take, at its key, with its default, so a copy changes nothing.

**What can stop a server that started on 0.14.0:**

- **An old and a new name given different values fail startup**, rather than one quietly winning: `MCP_PORT=4141` with `PUBLISHER_MCP_PORT=4242`, say, or a `retrieval.embedding.model` in the file that differs from `EMBEDDING_MODEL`. Values are compared after they are read, so a negated old name (`PUBLISHER_NO_MCP_CONFIG=1`) agrees with its positive new one (`PUBLISHER_MCP_CONFIG_FILE_ENABLED=false`).
- **On Kubernetes, set `enableServiceLinks: false` on the pod.** Kubernetes sets `<SERVICE>_PORT=tcp://…` for every Service in the namespace, so a Service named `publisher-mcp` sets `PUBLISHER_MCP_PORT`, now `mcp.port`'s variable, and startup fails. The message names the Service.
- **The image uses the current names**, so a plain boot logs no deprecation warning. It sets `PUBLISHER_MCP_CONFIG_FILE_ENABLED=false` in place of `PUBLISHER_NO_MCP_CONFIG=1`, and its CMD passes `--root /publisher` in place of `--server_root /publisher`. To turn the `.mcp.json` write back on, pass `-e PUBLISHER_MCP_CONFIG_FILE_ENABLED=true`: `-e PUBLISHER_NO_MCP_CONFIG=` no longer does. `PUBLISHER_NO_MCP_CONFIG=0` or a `SERVER_ROOT` other than `/publisher` now fails startup, since each disagrees with the image's own value.
- **A `retrieval` key of the wrong type** (`"timeoutMs": "soon"`, an unknown provider) now fails startup like any setting's; in 0.14.0 the server stayed up with the block refused and `/status` naming it. A block that fails as a whole (a `vertex` provider without `projectId`) still does that, and its message now ends with where each of its keys came from.
- **A secret in the file must be one `${VAR}` reference and nothing else**: a literal, or a literal around a reference, fails startup. A reference to an unset variable fails startup only when no flag or variable gives the setting.

**Deprecated, still working:** every old name logs a warning naming its replacement and counts in `publisher_deprecated_usage_total{feature="config:<old name>"}`, so you can find what still sets one. A release after the next refuses them. Names the design left unchanged, such as `PUBLISHER_PORT` and `--port`, are not deprecated, and neither are `--init` and `--watch-env`, which are kept as short forms of `--initialize-storage` and `--watch-environments`. `MCP_APP_ORIGIN` and `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE` become `PUBLISHER_MCP_APP_ORIGIN` and `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE_ENABLED`.

**Other changes:**

- **One precedence for every setting: flag, then variable, then file.** Two cases change: a `retrieval.embedding` key in the file no longer wins over a variable (`PUBLISHER_RETRIEVAL_EMBEDDING_MODEL`, `_BASE_URL` and `_DIMENSIONS` win over `model`, `baseUrl` and `dimensions`; a Google or Vertex provider still ignores the three old `EMBEDDING_*` variables), and `--watch-env` replaces `PUBLISHER_WATCH` instead of adding to it.
- **`useBundledDefault` counts the variables.** `SERVER_ROOT=/x` (or `PUBLISHER_ROOT`) now turns off the bundled sample config, as `--server_root` already did.
- **Every setting can be in the file**, except the launch settings (`root`, `config`, `useBundledDefault`, `initializeStorage`, `watchEnvironments`), which startup warns about there. `retrieval.embedding` and `retrieval.llm` now accept their `apiKey`, and `retrieval.embedding` accepts `minSimilarity` and `connectionSchemaIndexingEnabled`.
- **Every key of the `retrieval` block has a variable and a flag**, derived from its key (`retrieval.llm.provider` is `PUBLISHER_RETRIEVAL_LLM_PROVIDER` and `--retrieval-llm-provider`). `retrieval.indexing.maxEntities`, which does nothing, gets none. The block is put together from every source and then checked as one object, and a refusal ends with where each key it concerns came from.
- **A boolean flag takes no value.** `--allow-proxy-connections false` turns proxy connections on, as it did before; startup now warns that the `false` is ignored and names `--no-allow-proxy-connections`.
- A secret has no flag, and is never logged or echoed in an error. `packageVersioning`, `packageInlineFields` and `modelPage` have no flag either.

## [0.15.0] — (BREAKING) a version a host has bound keeps its manifest, and is never served from this server's own runs

**Fixed: a version bound to a host manifest lost it on a reload.** A bind that recompiled or rebound a published version re-read `manifestLocation` from the version's `publisher.json`, which usually names none, so the version reported no manifest although it was serving one, and this server's own run-store entries were then laid over it, replacing the host manifest's database tables with this server's tables for the same sources. A version now keeps the manifest its registry row names through every bind, and serves the host's tables. Only servers that both bind versions to a host manifest and run materializations locally were affected.

**Fixed: clearing a host-bound version's manifest could serve tables the host had retired.** A host clears a version's `manifestLocation` (`PUT …/versions/{version}/manifest` with null, or `{}`) to say "answer live", typically just before it drops those tables. In 0.14.0 the next reload or restart bound whatever this server's own run store held for it, including the output of builds the host instructed, and reported `manifestBindingStatus` `bound` with a null `boundManifestUri`, so a host checking for drift saw nothing to correct.

The rule: a host owns a version once a manifest it named (by that route or by a publish) has actually bound, or a run it instructed with `buildInstructions` has run, even one whose commit failed. A manifest whose fetch fails, such as a mistyped URL, marks nothing. The version's record keeps the mark across an unload and a restart; nothing clears it. Such a version, cleared, serves live at once and through every reload and restart until the host binds a manifest again; its status reads `unbound`, with `manifestEntryCount` 0 and a null `boundManifestUri`. **The cost:** a version built with `buildInstructions` serves live after a clear, a reload or a restart until a host binds a manifest to it, even if the host never meant to bind one.

A version no host has bound or built, as on a standalone server, serves what its own runs built when its binding is cleared, at once rather than after the next local run, falling back to live when its run store holds nothing. A PATCH clearing an unversioned package's `manifestLocation` does the same only where unversioned packages restore from the local store on load (an environment reloaded from the database at startup); elsewhere it goes live, as before.

**On upgrade,** a stored version counts as the host's when its row names a manifest or it has a run with `buildInstructions` recorded on this server, so such a version cleared under an earlier release goes live at its next load. The upgrade reads only the stored row, so it marks a version whose row names a manifest even if that manifest never bound (a mistyped URL, say); from then on only a manifest that binds marks one. Any other version cleared under an earlier release keeps binding its own run store until a host binds it.

**Who was affected:** deployments where a host binds versions to manifests and clears them, and this server's run store holds builds of those versions (a host-instructed build leaves its output there). A standalone server, or a host that never clears a binding, sees no change.

**Contract change: a local run of a host-bound package or version answers 409.** It would build tables it cannot serve. A run that passes `buildInstructions` is still accepted, and the scheduler already skipped such a package. `malloy-pub materialize` exits 1 on the refusal. If a host manifest is bound while a run builds, the run commits but reports `autoLoad: "failed"`, and `--wait` exits 2.

**Also fixed:** a publish that bound a new manifest bound it a second time, and a run's own published version recompiled a second time just after `MANIFEST_FILE_READY`, changing its `servedRevision` again. Each now binds once.

## [0.15.0] — (BREAKING) a storage refusal answers 403 and no storage URL reaches a caller or a log

**Contract change: a storage refusal answers 403 `STORAGE_ACCESS_DENIED` or `PATH_ACCESS_DENIED`.** When an object store refuses the database's read (a DuckLake data path, a bucket, an Azure container), the query route answered a 400 quoting the object's URL and the raw `sqlQuery` route an outage's 502. Both now answer 403, naming the source or connection and no URL; the access record reads it as `error`. The reason says who fixes it: `STORAGE_ACCESS_DENIED` when the URL lies under a data path the environment configures (the operator's storage credentials), and `PATH_ACCESS_DENIED` for a path the query or the model names itself (the path, or the caller's grant to it). Other warehouse rejections on `sqlQuery` keep their status.

**No storage URL reaches a caller on any other path either:** a 4xx carrying driver text, a Malloy error body, compile diagnostics (REST and `compile_model`), MCP error text, a run's recorded `error`, `failures[].reason` and `autoLoadError`, and `/status` `loadErrors` replace each URL with `<storage path>`.

**The server log masks secrets on every line.** The full error text is logged, with a signed URL's signature, credential and token, and a Postgres password, masked in values and keys, nested errors and cycles included, however the URL's separators are escaped or encoded. Masking never alters a logged object, and a call to the server's logger never throws.

## [0.15.0] — security fix: a stored table could answer a caller with rows live would not

Several cases let a stored table answer a caller with rows that live would not return to that caller, mostly past a source's own row-level gate (`#(access_filter)`, which Publisher reads past with the gated-sources switch off for a source's own gate, or with `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE_GATED_SOURCES` on). Each is fixed by answering such queries live, or by reading the right column. Upgrade if any applies to you. As with every gate, these hold only behind the gateway that sets the givens from a verified identity ([operating model](docs/security-posture.md#operating-model-a-microservice-behind-your-gateway)).

**Fixed: a caller's query time zone could move a gate over a stored time value.** A gate that compares a time value computed in a query stage of the source (a day or other truncation stored as a column), on a `#@ persist` or `#(materialize)` table in the database or in a `storage=` destination, was judged for time-zone safety by the fields the caller's query read, never the fields the gate read. A query that set its own `timezone:` could then be answered from the table with another time period's rows. A gated rollup whose grain holds such a value had the same blind spot.
