Each environment now keeps a status snapshot current as it changes: a package copy's metadata is captured when a load, reload, install, bind or metadata PATCH of it settles, and a package's version rows are re-read after each write to them. A poll reads that snapshot and what the server already holds in memory, and builds no metadata, reads nothing from the database and starts no load. In a benchmark of 3 environments × 8 packages × 3 versions, the server's CPU time per poll fell from about 8 ms to about 1 ms.

The body is unchanged, field for field, including `includeLoading=true`. Two differences in timing, neither of a field a reconcile reads: with inline fields on, a package entry's metadata (its warnings, `buildPlan`, description) is as of the last load, reload, bind or PATCH of that package, while `status` and the manifest-binding fields are read live on every poll as before; and a package registered from the config that nothing has loaded yet is no longer loaded, or listed, by a `/status` poll. Startup loads every configured package itself, so this is only a package registered and not yet loaded; the first request that names it, a listing of its environment, or a reload loads it as before. (A package whose startup load failed was not retried by polls before either.)

The snapshot makes `/status` cheap with `PUBLISHER_PACKAGE_INLINE_FIELDS` on or off. With it on, the body still carries every entry's full metadata, about 357 KB per poll for 480 versions, so a fleet polling often may still want it `off` to save bandwidth.

## [0.14.0] — re-binding the same build manifest no longer recompiles the package

Workers in Credible's dev fleet on 0.13.1 looped reloads: the control plane re-binds a version's build manifest whenever a heartbeat does not show it bound, and every such bind, even of the manifest the package was already serving, recompiled every model in the load pool and then every model's served copy on the main thread. With the main thread busy, `/status` heartbeats timed out, which made the control plane re-bind and reload again.

Binding a version (or a package loaded with a `manifestLocation`) to the manifest its models were last compiled against now fetches it and recompiles nothing; the binding is reported `bound` as before. A manifest that changed, a reload since, or another bind in between still recompiles. A `PATCH` that names a `manifestLocation` always reloads, as before, since it also applies the `publisher.json` it writes. When a package does recompile against a manifest, each model's served copy compiles once instead of starting, being discarded and starting again; a served copy with no table to read compiles nothing; and a source whose re-root does not compile is not recompiled or warned about again for the same model and tables (for ten minutes) — it keeps answering live, as it did. The served copy hands the event loop a turn between its compile passes.

Answers are unchanged: the same sources are served from the same tables. No API, enum or metric value changes.

## [0.14.0] — less main-thread work per package load

0.13.1 added a check to every package load that walked each model's whole compiled definition for joins inside array queries. That walk ran on the main thread, and it remembered every node it visited in a table that outlived the walk. The check now asks first whether a model governs access at all. A model that governs nothing is not walked for joins. A model that does is walked once, and the walk keeps nothing afterwards. A load that refused such a join still refuses it, with the same message.

The memory governor reads only the process's resident memory on each tick, not the full `process.memoryUsage()` object with its heap statistics. In Bun those statistics cost more as the heap grows.

The render-tag check now keeps its findings for each model, keyed on a digest of the results it reads. A model loaded again unchanged reuses its findings instead of being checked again on the main thread. A change to the model's text or to the schema of a table it reads is checked afresh. The cache lives in the server process, so a new `@malloydata/render-validator` is checked afresh after the restart that installs it. The cache holds the findings of at most 1,024 models. The warnings a package reports are unchanged.

No API, enum or metric value changes.

## [0.14.0] — colocated and `storage=` tables answer five shapes the same way

Five shapes were answered differently by a colocated table and a `storage=` one, by accident rather than for any reason inherent to where the table lives. Each now gives the same outcome in both tiers, equal to live:

- **A colocated `#(materialize)` source with a zoned timestamp column is served.** Its table was bound from the plan's columns alone, which leave a `timestamptz` out, so the whole source was answered live (a `column_types` problem). It is now bound from the plan's columns, whose types stay authoritative, plus each zoned timestamp column its build read back from the table it wrote, which the plan cannot spell; that column is declared as live types it, as on a `storage=` table. A planned column live types as warehouse-native (a UUID) that the build could not spell is left out, so only a query that reads it is answered live. A table built before its build read its columns back is bound from the plan alone, as before.
- **Two colocated pair tables whose sources compile to the same SQL are each served.** Sources that differ only in their gates or their `name=` share one colocated table at one content address, and the served copy read that shared table as a pair table read through a join, so their child measures were answered live. A query that reads the shared table once, as one of those sources, is now served from it, as a `storage=` source is from its own table. One that reads it more than once is still answered live.
- **A `storage=` rollup read beside a `join_one` is served once its key is checked.** A query that aggregates the querying source's own rows beside a `join_one` to a rollup (`flight_count` beside `crew.crew_size`) is served only when the rollup's build checked the join's key unique. That check was planned for a colocated rollup only, so in a `storage=` destination the query was always answered live (`COUNT_SEMANTICS`). The build now runs it for a `storage=` rollup too, over the base's rows on their own connection, and records it against the table in the destination. A repeated key warns `preaggregate-join-one-key-repeated` there as well, and is answered live. In both tiers, a rollup whose build read a stored upstream's table instead of the base's rows (a base that is itself stored) now records no check, since the base's rows may not be the rows it grouped, so such a query is answered live; before, a colocated one could record a pass over the base's rows while its stored copy held a repeated key.
- **A zoned `storage=` rollup that no join can read is no longer built.** A rollup over a source with its own `timezone:` is read only through a join from a source in the same zone. A `storage=` one is read that way only when that source is stored in the same destination. Otherwise it was built and never read, with no warning. It is now refused at plan with `preaggregate-time-zone`, as a colocated one with no such joiner is, and its measures are answered live.
- **A colocated incremental pair table outside DuckDB says it rebuilds in full.** A pair table's delta is applied only in DuckDB, so a colocated one in another warehouse (Postgres, Snowflake, BigQuery) was rebuilt in full on every refresh, silently. Its plan now carries no incremental keys, and the package warns `materialize-pair-full-refresh`, naming why and suggesting `storage=`. It is still built and served, as before. The plan no longer stores the pair table's `__pair_watermark` column there, so the table's content address moves: each such table (colocated, incremental, in Postgres, Snowflake or BigQuery) is rebuilt once by its next run, and its queries are answered live until then.

No API, enum or metric value changes.

## [0.14.0] — a colocated `#(materialize)` source behind its own row-level gate is built and served, as a colocated `#@ persist` is

A `#(materialize)` source with no `storage=`, whose own `#(access_filter)` or row-level `#(authorize)` is proven to be its entry point's own row filter or lock, is now built in its own warehouse and served from that table with `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE_GATED_SOURCES` off, the default. The gate is re-applied when the table is read: it is grafted onto every served query and proven there exactly as on live, so each caller gets live's rows, or live's denial. The table holds every caller's rows and never leaves the author's warehouse, which is why a colocated v1 `#@ persist` has been served this way since the v1 cutover; `#(materialize)` now follows the same rule. Before, it was refused (`persist-source-refused`, reason `authorize`) and answered live.

Nothing else moves. A `#(materialize) storage=` source behind a gate still needs `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE_GATED_SOURCES` on, and is refused without it. A gate the source inherits from one it extends, one reached through a join, and a gate over a source whose build would substitute a given stay refused on every tier, and an answer that would also read a `storage=` table is answered live. A model with no gated colocated `#(materialize)` source behaves exactly as before. As with every gate, it holds only behind the gateway that sets the givens from a verified identity ([operating model](docs/security-posture.md#operating-model-a-microservice-behind-your-gateway)).

## [0.14.0] — a `storage=` rollup returns exact big-integer sums and keeps `timestamptz` grains

A rollup stored in a `storage=` destination (`#(preaggregate)` or v1 `#@ preaggregate`) read its stored table with the wrong types in two cases. A big-integer measure (a `sum` of a BIGINT) whose total passed 2^53 came back rounded, as `-9007199254740992` where live gives `-9007199254740993`; it is now read through its native type and returns every digit, as live does. A grain dimension live types as `timestamptz` came back typed `timestamp`, with equal rows; it now keeps its `timestamptz` type. A big-integer column the destination stored where no cast reads it exactly (a float, its digits already lost) is no longer served: the rollup is skipped with reason `MISSING_FIELD` and the query is answered live. Colocated rollups are unchanged; they were already exact.

No API, enum or metric value changes.

## [0.14.0] — a `#@ preaggregate` rollup over a stored base builds and serves, as documented now

A `#@ preaggregate` on a measure of a source that is itself `#@ persist storage=` builds and serves, with no change to the model. It has since 0.13.0, when the v1 cutover began reading each `#@ preaggregate` line as the `#(preaggregate)` it spells: that rollup is built from the author's rows, never from the base's stored table, so neither reason such rollups were once left out holds. The documentation still said they were left out with a `preaggregate-over-stored-base` warning; it now says what happens, and the code that would have left them out, which nothing reached any more, is removed.

What happens: each grain is planned, built and served exactly as the `#(preaggregate)` would be, with the same build and the same content address, one table per grain under the rollup's readable name (`<package>__<file>__<base>_by_<grain>__p<hash>`, never the base's), in the destination its own `storage=` names or alongside the base without one. A query a rollup covers is answered from it, equal to live; a query-shaped base keeps building and answering everything else from its own stored table. The refusals are the rollup leg's, for the same reasons as `#(preaggregate)`: a base whose rows read a given or the current time, or a gated base the gated-sources switch does not cover, builds no rollup and warns. A table extended with measures still cannot carry `#@ persist`: under this release such a package fails to load (`persist-not-materializable`; see "an invalid materialization annotation fails the load, everywhere" above), and its rollups build once that `#@ persist` is removed.

Nothing that is built or served changes, and no rollup's address or table moves. The `preaggregate-over-stored-base` warning code and the `rollup_over_stored_base` serve verdict reason were already never reported, and still are not; a client may stop handling them.

## [0.14.0] — a source sharing a table with a refused sibling no longer builds over another package's table

Two stored sources that compile to the same build share one table, named after the first of them. When that first source has a `name=` and the table at that name is not provably this package's (another package marked it as its own, or no run of this package wrote it, as with a user's own table), the auto-run refused that source and left the table alone, but then built the same table for the sibling sharing it, replacing that table's rows and removing its mark. The refusal now belongs to the table. Every source sharing it is refused with the same `table-owned-elsewhere` (or `table-ownership-unverified`) reason, nothing is written, the table and its mark stay as they were, and each of those sources is answered live. This holds for colocated tables and `storage=` destinations, and for `scope: "package"` versions. When the name is free, the shared table is built once and marked as this package's, whichever source builds it.

No API, enum or metric value changes.

## [0.14.0] — a rollup a compile-time gate refuses now warns `preaggregate-not-built`

This changes the meaning of a signal. A valid `#(preaggregate)` or `#@ preaggregate` rollup that a compile-time gate refuses alone, while the rest of the package loads, used to carry the `persist-source-refused` warning of a `#@ persist` source, though its author wrote no `#@ persist`. It now carries its own code, `preaggregate-not-built` (severity `warn`), with `subject` its base source (now also when the refusal left the rollup out of the plan's `sources`), and a message that names the base and the grain before the gate's reason: `#(preaggregate) rollup of source "orders" at (category) is not built, so its measures are served live: …`, worded as the `preaggregate-reads-given` message. The gates are the ones that refuse a rollup in the build plan's `refusedSources` (tier `preaggregate`): a dialect whose connection creates no table, a table name another rollup's table holds, a base scoped by a given, a row-level gate on a v1 rollup's base, and the `storage=` destination gate. `persist-source-refused` now means a `#@ persist` source only.

Nothing else changes: the same rollups are built or refused, the same queries are served or answered live, and `refusedSources` lists the same entries with the same reasons and messages. A rollup refusal that already had a code of its own keeps it (`preaggregate-access-filter`, `preaggregate-time-zone`, `preaggregate-current-time`, `preaggregate-reads-given`, `preaggregate-over-stored-base` and the like), and `preaggregate-malformed` is unchanged. Who is affected: a client that matched `persist-source-refused` to find refused rollups. Match `preaggregate-not-built` as well; warning codes are open strings, so a client that does not know the new code should show it as it shows any other warning.

## [0.14.0] — tables built in Credible now serve in three shapes that answered live

Three shapes of stored source had their tables built but were answered live, with a warning or none. Each now reads its table, with answers equal to live:

- **An index that exports a source whose join is left out.** A curating `index.malloy` that `export`s a source stored where one of its joins cannot reach (a join to a source on another connection) failed its whole served copy with `Cannot export`, so every stored source it publishes answered live. The join is now left out there as it is in the source's own file: queries that use it are answered live, and the rest read the table.
- **A colocated BigQuery table with no captured column types.** A colocated table whose manifest entry carries no `nativeSchema` (an entry written before the control plane recorded it) left every big-integer column out, and the source fell back to live with a `column_types` warning. On BigQuery such a column is now read through `INT64`, BigQuery's only integer type, so it is exact. On every other dialect nothing changes: without a captured type, the column is still left out.
- **A connection's SQL curated by an `include`.** A v1 `#@ persist` source declared as `conn.sql("…") include { … } extend { … }` was silently left as written. Its re-root now keeps both blocks, as for a query-shaped source. A connection-rooted declaration the served copy still cannot re-root now carries a `served-copy-not-served` warning instead of none. That includes a `storage=` source of a connection's SQL whose `include` hides a column (`private:` or `internal:`): a v1 `storage=` table stores public columns only, so it still answers live, and it now warns where it used to be silent, naming the column and what to change (make it public, keep the source colocated, or use `#(materialize)`). The query-shaped form (`… -> { … } include { private: … }`) gets the same warning in place of one that called it a Publisher bug.

A colocated source bound with no recorded type for a big-integer column, on any dialect, now also gets a new package warning, `stored-native-schema-missing`, naming its big-integer columns and whether each is read as `INT64` or answered live. The next full rebuild records the types and clears it.

API addition: the package warning code `stored-native-schema-missing`. No field or enum value is added.

## [0.14.0] — readable names for the tables Publisher names itself

A table Publisher names itself (a `#@ persist` or `#(materialize)` source with no `name=`, a persisted view, a rollup, and every table under `scope: "version"`) now says what it is in a warehouse listing: `<package>__<file>__<source>[__v<version>]__p<8 hex>`, for example `ecommerce__orders__order_summary__pda155503` where the table used to be `order_summary__p3f9c2a1b`. `<file>` is the model's base name; a persisted view reads `<source>_<view>` and a rollup `<base>_by_<grain>`; the hex is a hash of the environment, package, model path, source and version, so packages and environments sharing a schema still never share a table. The name fits each warehouse's identifier limit (50 characters on Postgres, Redshift, MySQL, Trino and Presto), cutting the package and file before the source. A hosted deployment names its tables with the same prefix.

- **A `name=` still wins.** In an unversioned or `scope: "package"` package a `name=` is the table's exact name, unchanged. Under `scope: "version"`, a `name=` sets the start of the table's name, schema included: `name="analytics.summary_t"` builds `analytics.summary_t__v1_2_0__p<8 hex>`, where it used to be `analytics.summary_t__v1_2_0_<8 hex>`. The `name=` part is sanitized like the rest and, if the name is too long for the warehouse, cut; the version and hash never are.
- **Existing tables are renamed on their next build.** A default-named table keeps serving until its source's next auto-run, scheduled or on demand, which builds it under its readable name. An incremental source stays at its old name, and keeps building incrementally there, until it is next reseeded, which builds it in full under the new one. Once that run has committed and every loaded copy of the package is bound to it, the old table is dropped only when Publisher can prove it is its own: the name is exactly the one it gave that source in this package, this package's earlier run built it for the same source and place, the replacement committed and is served, no other package has marked it since, and no other version's run still names it. Otherwise it is left, and the server log names the check that kept it; a table left because the server stopped, the drop failed or left it in place, the bind failed, or a check that may yet pass (the replacement not committed or not yet served, another run still naming it) is tried again by later runs. The checks read one server's records, so **servers that share a schema must upgrade together**. Anything that reads a default-named table by name outside Malloy must move to the new name; give the source a `name=` if it needs a fixed one.
- **A readable name sticks.** Once built, a table keeps its name while its source keeps its content address and place: moving or renaming a model file, or another source coming to share the table, does not rename it. `<file>` is the model that declares the source, not the last one that imports it; the build plan's `modelPath` for a `#@ persist` source now names the declaring model too, where it could name an importing one.
- **A run never builds two sources into one readable name.** Two sources' names can meet when two sources of one model share a name (a `#@ persist` source named like a persisted view's generated build source beside it, which the package also warns about), or on a hash collision. A table keeps a name it was built under only while no other source of the run takes that name fresh, so renaming a source beside a new source of its old name moves the renamed one rather than locking the new one out. The second source is not built and is answered live, and the run records it under `metadata.refusedSources` with a new reason, `table_name_collision`, also a new value of the `reason` label on `publisher_materialization_eligibility_refused_total`.
- **Two models with the same base name** in different directories give names that differ only in the hash. Rename one file if people browse the schema by name.

## [0.14.0] — a stored table built in another zone, read through a join, answers live

A `#(materialize)` table holds its zone-dependent values (a computed dimension such as `hour(ts)`, a truncation) as its build computed them, in its source's zone, its own or one it inherits. Read through a join, Malloy does not apply the joined source's `timezone:`, so a query that set no zone read the table in UTC while the table held, say, New York's values. The served copy answered it from the table and returned wrong rows: hours 16 to 21 where live gives 21 to 23 and 0 to 2. Such a query now answers live, with the `TIME_ZONE` reason.

The rule, for every value a table stores that depends on the zone:

- **The read zone.** A query reads its tables in the zone its first stage computes in: its own `timezone:`, else the zone its source sets or inherits, else the default. Every other zone it sets, in a later stage or a nest, is compared too. A table reached through a join is read in that same zone.
- **The build zone.** Each table was built in its stored source's zone, read from the author's model, where a zone the source inherits is kept.
- **Decided per column.** A query is answered live only when it reads one of the table's zone-dependent columns (a computed dimension the probe compiler did not clear, or a restated truncation) in another zone. A query that reads none, such as a measure of `amt` through the join, stays on the table.
- **Decided per table.** Only when the rows themselves depend on the zone does any read in another zone answer live: a zone-dependent `where:`, a rolling window, or a joined source stored as a record.
- **Same-zone reads stay served.** For example, a join read under the query's own `timezone:` that matches the zone the table was built in.
- **`'UTC'` and its aliases.** Only the spelling `'UTC'` counts as the default zone. An alias such as `'Etc/UTC'` is another zone, and answers live, because a dialect may not know it (MySQL without its time zone tables converts it to NULL).
- **An unknown stored source** is treated as built in an unknown zone, so a query that reads its zone-dependent values answers live.
- **A `#(materialize)` source with its own zone now keeps its timestamp truncations.** They are judged by the same rule, so `mzny -> { group_by: ts_day }` stays served. A query-shaped source that sets a zone still leaves them out, because its query's zone does not reach a query over it.

**A source that inherits its zone now computes in it.** A `#(materialize)` source that inherits its zone from its base (`inh is ny_base extend { … }`, with the base in the same file or another) was answered by the served copy in UTC. The re-root replaced that base with the stored table and dropped the zone, so an `hour(ts)`, a truncation and a time-literal filter came back in UTC where live answers in New York. This was wrong on main for a base in the same file. The re-root now writes the author's zone again. As a backstop, any query whose source computes in another zone in the served copy than in the author's model answers live. The same holds for a query-shaped source whose query inherits its base's zone (`ny_base -> { group_by: d is ts.day }`). It stored the truncation in New York and the served copy re-truncated it in UTC, which was also wrong on main. Such a truncation is now left out of the table, so a query that reads it answers live, and any other query stays served.

The decline messages now say the query reads a table, or a value, "in another time zone than it was built in". No table is rebuilt or re-addressed, and no API change.

## [0.14.0] — the remaining lookups through a package author's links stay inside the package

Every lookup Publisher makes through a path a package author controls now resolves it with the walk that confines model imports, which never looks at a path outside the package. A link that leads out, or out and back through another directory, gets the same answer whether or not what it passes through exists:

- **HTML data apps.** `public/` itself is now confined to the package: a `public/` that is a symlink out of the package serves and lists nothing (403), whatever it leads to. Before, its target was treated as the package's own, so `public -> /` served any file the server could read. A `public/` that links inside the package (`public -> web`) still serves. A link in `public/` that leads out answers 403 whether or not its target exists (before, 403 when it existed and 404 when it did not), and is left out of the data-app listing, which no longer opens such a page for its title.
- **Package listing.** A directory link that passes out of the package and back is listed as itself, so whether the outside directory exists no longer decides whether the package loads.
- **Retrieval prompts** (`retrieval.prompts.*` in `publisher.json`), **package and agent skills** (the skills directory, a skill directory, `reference/`, an agent's skills root and its assets), and **the report write path** (`PUT …/models/{path}`) refuse a link out the same way whatever it leads to. One visible change: a `skills/` that is a dangling link out of the package (`skills -> /absent`) is now reported as leading outside the package, which blocks the package's skills, where it used to be skipped silently; a dangling link inside the package is still skipped.
- **A walk that stops at a missing directory** opens only that point and the next name, so a directory appearing there afterwards cannot carry the open out of the package. Its error reads as the kernel's would (`f.md/..` fails with ENOTDIR).
- **Data probe errors** (`GET …/databases`) name the file by its package-relative path with the connection's reason, rather than echoing the SQL the probe compiled; a path inside Malloy's escaped quotes is no longer mangled (`'bad.parquet/'`).

No API change.

## [0.14.0] — an auto-run reports `MANIFEST_FILE_READY` only once its package serves the new tables

A materialization auto-run used to report `MANIFEST_FILE_READY` and then load its manifest into the package. A caller that waited for `MANIFEST_FILE_READY` (the REST `GET …/materializations/{id}`, `malloy-pub materialize --wait`, the Console) and queried at once could be answered live, or from the previous table, until the load finished.

Now the run records its manifest when it reaches `MANIFEST_ROWS_READY`, loads it into its package, and only then reports `MANIFEST_FILE_READY`, so a query sent after it is answered from the new tables. The load and that last move happen under the package's lock, so a reload or publish that lands meanwhile waits for them and binds the new manifest, not the one before it.

The run's `metadata` says how the load went: `autoLoad: "loaded"`, or `autoLoad: "failed"` with `autoLoadStep` (`reload`, `bind` or `timeout`) and `autoLoadError`. A failed load also sets the run's `error` ("Built, but not served …"). Such a run still settles at `MANIFEST_FILE_READY`, since its tables were built:

- `malloy-pub materialize --wait` prints "built but not served" and exits **2** for it, where it used to print "ready" and exit 0. A script that treats any non-zero exit as a failed build should treat 2 as "built, not yet served".
- The Console shows it as a warning, "Built, not served", not as done.
- What the package serves meanwhile depends on the step: after `reload` it keeps the models it had; after `bind` the run's colocated tables are served and its `storage=` ones are not. The package's next reload or restart binds the run's manifest either way.

Also:

- A load that has not finished after ten minutes settles the run as `autoLoad: "failed"`, `autoLoadStep: "timeout"`, so a hung load no longer holds the package's build slot until a restart.
- A stop that lands while the manifest loads does not cut the load short; the run settles at `MANIFEST_FILE_READY` with `stopIgnored: true`.
- A run's `manifest` is now present from `MANIFEST_ROWS_READY`, not only from `MANIFEST_FILE_READY`.
- Other loaded versions that share the run's tables (`scope: "package"`) are rebound just after the run reports `MANIFEST_FILE_READY`, as before.
- An orchestrated run never loads its manifest (the host distributes it), so for it nothing changes.
- No status is added. `MANIFEST_ROWS_READY` now also spans the load, so a run can be seen there a little longer.

## [0.14.0] — `#@ persist` on a named query stores its result (`PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE`)

With `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE` on (the default), `#@ persist` on a top-level `query:` builds the query's result as a generated source, `<query>__query`, in the same companion as the file's persisted views, colocated or with `storage=`. Its table answers exactly the calls of the query, and answers them equal to live:

- **Served from the table:** REST and MCP `queryName`, a single-query report and a report tile naming the query, `run: q`, and `run: q -> { … }`. The answer keeps the query's name, its columns in order, each column's kind (an aggregate is still a measure) and annotations, its ordering and its render tags.
- **Answered live:** `run: q + { … }` (a refinement; the path report skips the table `MISSING_FIELD`), any use of `q` inside another definition, and a query text that, outside the call, names the run target, any named query, or any source from another file (`MISSING_FIELD`). A later stage that joins a source declared in another file answers live; join it in the model instead.
- **Fixes wrong rows from a persisted view.** The view leg on main answered a later stage that joined the view's source back (`run: fv -> by_c -> { extend: { join_many: f is fv … } }`), or a caller's source built over it, from the stored result, so the join read the stored rows: `f.count()` was 1 for every row. A text that, outside the call (in a later stage, or a definition before the `run:`), names the run target, any named query, or any source from another file now declines (`MISSING_FIELD`) and is answered live, on both the view and query legs; the caller's own definitions before the `run:`, a dimension-only `extend:` and a join to another source of the declaring file are still served.
- **Ordering:** rows that tie on `order_by:`, or a query or later stage with no `order_by:`, may come back in another order than live's.
- **Governance fails closed.** Not built, with `persist-query-not-built` naming why: a query that reads a given or the current time, whose source has a given-reading `where:`, and any query that reaches a row-level gate (`#(access_filter)` or `#(authorize)`: its source's own, one it inherits, or one on a source it joins), whatever `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE_GATED_SOURCES` says. Such a query is answered live under its gate, and the leg is never tried past an entry-point gate (`publisher_query_route_total` counts it `leg="query"`, `skipped`, `CONTRACT`).
- **Regrouped as a persisted view is.** The table answers with each measure a measure again by the persisted view's regroup rule: only when the last stage groups by at least one dimension and nests nothing. A query that aggregates with no `group_by:` is built but answered live (`MISSING_FIELD`); a result that nests is not built.
- **Changed meaning of a signal: a new `leg` value.** `publisher_query_route_total` gains `leg="query"`, which counts the persisted-query leg's routes (`used`, `skipped` with the path report's reason, `fallback`). This value is new. A persisted view's routes stay `leg="view"`. The path report names the table `kind: "query"`.
- **Not yet:** persisting a query from inside a report file.

**API addition.** `QueryPathTableKind` (the path report's `servedBy.kind` and each candidate's `kind`) gains `query`, a persisted named query's table. A client treats a kind it does not know as a stored table it cannot name. The build plan lists a persisted query as an ordinary persist source (`origin: persist`); its serve verdict reads `The persisted query \`<query>\``.

Off, nothing changes from the entry below: the query is warned `persist-query-not-built` and answered live.

## [0.14.0] — `#@ persist` on a named query says what it does

`#@ persist` on a top-level `query:` builds nothing: Malloy's persistence planner walks sources only. The package used to warn with the source warning, `persist-not-materializable`, which told the author to "persist a query source" about something that already is a query, and a materialization run over the whole package was refused because of it.

- **A dedicated warning.** The query now carries `persist-query-not-built` (`warn`, `subject` the query), which says it is answered live and names the workaround: persist a source over the query (`#@ persist` on `source: q_result is q`) and query that source. The code is an open string.
- **A misspelled key is reported.** An unknown or retired key on the query's `#@` line is reported as on a source (`persist-unknown-key`, `persist-retired-key`).
- **A build run is no longer refused.** A persisted query is not a dropped persist source, so it no longer fails a whole-package run.

No API change beyond the new warning code.

## [0.14.0] — error messages no longer include the server's filesystem paths

A package that failed to load at boot reported the compile error with the server's absolute path to the file (`FILE: file:///…/publisher_data/<env>/<pkg>/<version>/m.malloy`) in `/status` `loadErrors`, MCP `get_status` and `list_packages`, and the package resource; a refused publish (424) did too. A failed reload already named the file package-relative. Every package load, compile and recompile now names the package's files relative to the package root (`FILE: m.malloy`), and `compile` diagnostics carry a package-relative `at.url` instead of a `file://` URL. Any other server path in such a message (a file imported from outside the package, a configured location that did not mount) reads `<outside package>`, and a missing location is named by its package.

## [0.14.0] — BREAKING: a materialized source serves from its table only its own given-reading `where:`

**BREAKING (speed, not correctness).** A source scoped by a caller's given (`where: org_id = $ORG_ID`) is still built with that term left out and served from its table with the term applied for each caller, but only when the term is written on the materialized source itself. A given-reading `where:` the source inherits from a base is now refused at plan: the source is not built and is answered live, under the term, exactly as it answers without materialization. Nothing answers differently; some queries that read a table now run live.

- **`#(materialize)`** (materialization v2): a source that inherits its term from a base in the same file (one or several `extend` or rename hops up) used to be built and served by keeping that base's text in the served copy (#1688). It now gets a `materialize-not-built` warning that says to move the given-reading `where:` onto the materialized source itself. An extension that declares its own `#(materialize)` over a parent that writes such a term is refused the same way; the parent is still built, and the extension's queries are answered from the parent's table. A dimension declared on a base that reads a given or the current time now refuses the source too (a current-time one used to be built into a table no query read), and a time-zone-dependent one declared on a base is stored as built, so a query over that table that sets a time zone is answered live. That includes a query on a source that declares its own `timezone:` (or inherits one up its chain), which used to be answered from such a table in the build's zone, a wrong answer the older case of a zone-dependent dimension on a base in another file shared and which is fixed here too.
- **v1 `#@ persist`**, on both tiers: a source whose given-reading `where:` is inherited from a base was built but always answered live. It is now refused at plan and no longer built, so its verdict reads live, with the new reason `inherited_where_with_given`.
- **API addition:** `RefusedSource.reason` gains `inherited_where_with_given`, and the `publisher_materialization_eligibility_refused_total` metric can carry it as its `reason` label.

To keep a shape on a table, write the term on the source you materialize (`#(materialize)` on `tenant_orders is orders extend { where: org_id = $ORG_ID }`). Extensions of it that declare no `#(materialize)` read its table.

## [0.14.0] — a persisted view's answer reports its measures as measures

A query answered from a persisted view's table (`#@ persist` on a `view:`) returned the view's rows exactly, but every column as a dimension: a measure's `#(malloy)` result annotation lost `calculation` (and gained a drill `code`), so a renderer or chart reading the result saw dimensions where live returns measures. The view is now redeclared over its stored rows by grouping them again by its dimensions, each group one stored row, with each measure re-aggregated from its one stored value (a boolean measure keeps a NULL as NULL). The rows are unchanged, and each column now carries live's kind and annotations; only a stored column's `drill_expression` still names the stored column, as before.

That regrouping is exact only when the stored rows are keyed by the view's dimensions, so a persisted view that holds a measure or a nest is now answered from its table only when its last stage groups by at least one dimension and it has no nest. Any other such view is answered live, with the same rows and metadata as live: one with a measure and no dimension (`{ aggregate: … }`), one whose `select:` carries a `calculate:`, one with a `nest:` (with or without a measure beside it), and one with a measure of a type `max()` does not take (a JSON value, an array). These were served from the table before, with dimensions in place of measures. A view of dimensions alone, with no nest, is served as before. Its table is still built; to have it serve, give the view a dimension, or move the nest into a view of its own. No API change.

## [0.14.0] — (BREAKING) the `name=` view is removed; `name=` on `#(materialize)` still names and places the table

Materialization v2 (`PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE`, now on by default) no longer makes a view at a `#(materialize)` source's `name=`. That view gave a table named by its generation (a `scope: "version"` run's, or a host-orchestrated run's) a stable alias for readers outside Malloy; it is gone, and generation-named tables get no alias view. This removal is the breaking part. `name=` itself stays: on `#(materialize)` it names the table and places it in a schema or dataset, as on v1 `#@ persist`, which is unchanged.

- **What `name=` does on `#(materialize)`.** An unversioned or `scope: "package"` run writes the table at exactly that name, schema or dataset included, checked and marked as the package's own (`table-owned-elsewhere` and `table-ownership-unverified` refuse a name another package or an unknown holder has), as for v1 `#@ persist name=`. A `scope: "version"` run keeps the name's schema or dataset and gives its last segment the version's suffix, as v1 does. A host-orchestrated run writes the name the host assigns, in that name's container. None of them makes a view.
- **BREAKING: no view is created, repointed, restored or settled.** No build, commit or reclaim makes a `name=` view any more, and runs no longer record `metadata.nameViews` (free-form run metadata; older runs keep theirs). A reader outside Malloy that read a `scope: "version"` or host-orchestrated table through the view at `name=` must read the table itself, or read from an unversioned or `scope: "package"` package, whose table sits at `name=`.
- **A colocated `#(materialize)` no longer needs `name=`.** Without one, its table, like a `storage=` one's, is the source's name with its package's suffix (`<source>__p<8 hex>`), or its version's under `scope: "version"`; a source name that is not a plain table name (outside ASCII, or with a space) is folded to its plain characters plus a hash of the name. On BigQuery, where a table needs a dataset, a colocated `#(materialize)` with no `name=` is not built: a `materialize-not-built` warning says to give it a dataset-qualified `name=`.
- **A changed table name rebuilds.** A source whose table name changes (a `name=` added, removed or changed, or a v1 source moved to `#(materialize)` under another name) is rebuilt under the new name by the next self-instructed run, rather than carried forward at the old one. The old table stays with the runs that built it, and goes when they are deleted with their tables.
- **Collisions compare the names a run writes.** Two sources are refused as sharing a table (`materialize-not-built`, or the v1 collision refusal) only when the names the run actually writes meet: in an unversioned or `scope: "package"` package a defaulted name, which carries the package's suffix, never meets an author's `name=`, while under `scope: "version"`, where every name takes the version's suffix, a source with no `name=` and another whose `name=` equals its name do meet; and on a destination that folds case (DuckDB and every `storage=` destination, Trino, Presto, Databricks, SQL Server) `Orders` and `orders` meet. MySQL is compared as written, since whether it folds depends on the server's `lower_case_table_names`.
- **Views earlier releases left.** A warehouse or storage destination may still hold a view an earlier release made, carrying the comment `malloy-publisher:name-view owner=<environment>/<package> target=<table>`. Deleting a run with `dropTables=true`, or reclaiming an archived or deleted version's tables, drops such a view before the table it reads, only when the package's runs recorded it, it still carries that package's mark, and the warehouse confirms it reads that table and nothing else (Postgres from its dependencies, SQL Server from its expression dependencies, other dialects from its definition, an unqualified name read in the view's own schema); a view an operator repointed with `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`, which keeps the comment, or rewrote to join or filter on another relation, is left, and so is one whose reads cannot be proven. A `name=` build (v1 or `#(materialize)`, unversioned or `scope: "package"`) whose name holds the package's own marked view, still reading its marked table, replaces the view with its table: on DuckDB and Postgres in the swap's own transaction, so a failed build leaves the view, and elsewhere just before the build; on Postgres a reader's own view over it fails the build with an error saying so. A view with no mark, or another package's, is never touched. Any other leftover view stays: find it by its comment mark and drop it by hand once nothing reads it.

No API change: no field or enum value is added or removed.

## [0.14.0] — a package's Malloy imports stay inside the package

A package's models can no longer read files outside the package. Every file the compiler reads for a model (an `import`, a `.malloynb`, a data-styles file) must resolve, through `realpath`, to the package root or inside it; for a versioned package that root is the version's own directory. Before, `import "../other/x.malloy"` read a sibling package's model (with versioning off) or a file beside the version directory (with versioning on), and `import "/etc/..."` told the author whether an arbitrary path existed. Both are now refused with one fixed message, `imports must stay inside the package`, which names no path and reads the same whether or not the target exists. The rule holds on every compile: the load and its worker, a reload, `/compile` and MCP `compile_model` at each scope, the build plan, and the generated build and served-copy models.

A model or notebook file that is itself a symlink out of the package is refused with the same message, as a compile error (424), whether or not its target exists; before, a notebook link out was read and its text served, and a dangling link failed the load with a 500. The text Publisher reads back from a compiled model (served copy, chained `storage=` build, entity code) is read only from the files that model compiled from.

A package's `publisher.json` is read only as a file inside the package, and never written through a link: a manifest that links out of the package (to anything or to nothing), a directory or an unreadable file answers that the manifest does not exist, and an invalid manifest's error no longer quotes its content. A PATCH of a package whose `publisher.json` leads outside the package answers 400; one that links inside the package is replaced by the file itself. A report write onto a planted link is refused the same way whatever it leads to.

Copying a package (an install from a local location, an environment's packages at boot) now keeps symlinks as written, so a relative link inside the package keeps working in the copy. Before, the copy rewrote it to an absolute path into the source directory. A local install that relied on a relative link pointing _out_ of the package (which the copy used to turn into an absolute path into the source tree) now gets a link that dangles in the copy, and the file it named is not served: copy that file into the package instead.

What keeps working: imports between a package's own directories, `../` included (`import "../orders.malloy"` from a subfolder); a symlink inside the package that points inside it; a package mounted as a symlink under `--watch-env`; and virtual files such as a request's overlay and the generated companions. A model that imported a file from outside its package now fails to load with that message: copy the file into the package. SQL a model runs through DuckDB (`read_csv`, `read_parquet`, `read_text`) is not covered by this rule ([security-posture.md](docs/security-posture.md#known-gaps), gap 6).

## [0.14.0] — routing and bind metrics: one route counter, one bind counter

The serving metrics are renamed and folded so each counts one thing, in the vocabulary the path report already uses. Every label is a closed set, and none names a package, source, table or connection. What changes for a dashboard or alert:

- **`publisher_query_variant_routing_total{variant, outcome, reason}` is now `publisher_query_route_total{leg, outcome, reason}`.** `leg` is `view`, `rollup`, `served` or `live`. `outcome` is `used`, `skipped`, or `fallback`: a leg that answered and whose stored run then failed, so live answered (was `skipped` with `run_failed`). `reason` is `NONE` when used, `RUN_FAILED` with `fallback`, and otherwise the public `SkipReason` the query's path report gives: `row_level_gate` is now `CONTRACT`, and `does_not_answer` is the decline's own reason (`MISSING_FIELD` when it gives none). A leg that does not apply to the query (`not_applicable`) is no longer counted. `live` is counted `used` when it answered a query the router counted a leg for.
- **`publisher_storage_serve_routing_total` is removed.** Its outcomes are on the route counter: `storage` is `leg="served", outcome="used"`; `runtime_live_fallback` is `outcome="fallback"`; `blocked_by_row_level_gate` is `outcome="skipped", reason="CONTRACT"`, now counted per leg rather than once per query; its `live_fallback` has no counterpart (the leg's skip says why). Its `origin` label has none either, since `leg` separates a rollup from a stored source.
- **`publisher_storage_bindings_withheld_total` is removed,** into the route counter's `reason="STALE"`. A table past its freshness window is left out of the query's pin and the query is read live; the leg that would have read it (the served copy, a rollup or a persisted view) is counted `skipped` with `STALE`, which is what the path report says. It counts queries, where the old counter counted tables.
- **`publisher_materialization_manifest_bind_total{outcome}` and `publisher_materialization_colocated_bind_dropped_total{reason}` are now `publisher_served_copy_bind_total{scope, outcome, reason}`.** A manifest bind is `scope="manifest"` with the same `success`, `failure` and `timeout` outcomes and `reason="none"`. Each source entry a bind decides is `scope="source"`: `bound`, `partial` (it serves, with a join read as written or left out) or `declined`; a decline's `reason` keeps `build_plan_unavailable` and `refused`, adds `missing_table` (the table bound under the source's name was built from another definition), and adds the served copy's reasons, which until now only its `served-copy-not-served` package warning reported (`compile_failed`, `column_types`, `fields_not_carried`, `read_terms_not_kept`, `classification_not_kept` and the rest). The units differ by who counts: a bind counts once per stored table per bind, and the served copy once per source per model per snapshot it compiles, `declined` beating `partial` (a source two models read counts twice, so the outcomes are not a count of sources). The served copy's `inline_join_kept` (the join is kept as written and read through the join) and `cross_connection_join` (the join is left out, and a query that reads it is answered live) count as `partial` while the source is still served. An extension table that falls back to its own blocks (`compile_failed`, `reroot_not_compiled`) may still serve, and is counted `declined`. `reason="build_plan_unavailable"` is still the one to alert on.

No API change: `servedFrom` keeps its values, and its description now names the route counter's `fallback` as the same event as its `live_fallback`.

## [0.14.0] — (BREAKING) materialization v2 is on by default (`PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE`)

`PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE` (`materialize.enabled`) now defaults to `true`. Materialization v2 used to need it set explicitly; a server that never set it now runs v2. With it on, Publisher reads `#(materialize)` on a source and `#(preaggregate)` on a measure, plans each in the package's build plan under the author's source name, builds them, and serves them: a `#(materialize)` table through the served copy (the author's own files, with the source re-rooted on its stored table), a `#(preaggregate)` rollup through the rollup leg, including a query that reads its measures through a join, and `#@ persist` on a view through the persisted-view leg, which answers a query that calls that view exactly. A colocated `#(materialize)` is served with this switch alone; a `storage=` one still needs `PERSIST_STORAGE_MODE=on`, which is unchanged and off by default. `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE_GATED_SOURCES` is a separate setting and stays off: a query through a row-level gate is still never answered from a `storage=` table.

What an operator sees on a server that did not set the switch before:

- **Packages that use only v1 annotations.** Their `#@ persist` sources and `#@ preaggregate` rollups are planned, built and served exactly as before. Each measure with `#@ preaggregate` now carries a `deprecated-preaggregate-annotation` package warning naming its v2 spelling, `#(preaggregate)`; it still works. A `#@ persist` on a **view** was ignored before and is now planned and built as a table of its own, so a package with one gains a build-plan entry and a table its builds write.
- **Packages with v2 annotations, or `#@ persist` on a view (BREAKING).** A `#(materialize)` or `#(preaggregate)` line used to be ignored (a `#(preaggregate)` drew an `annotation-near-miss` warning), and so did `#@ persist` on a view. Each is now planned, built and checked, and its sources answer from their tables where the path report says so. The checks can refuse a package that published yesterday:
  - **Refused at publish, and at load.** A malformed v2 declaration: an unknown key on `#(materialize)` or `#(preaggregate)` (`materialize-unknown-key`, `preaggregate-unknown-key`), a `#(materialize)` line that does not parse (`materialize-unparseable`), or a `#(preaggregate)` on a field that is not a measure (`preaggregate-not-a-measure`), whose grain names a field that is not a dimension of the source (`preaggregate-unknown-grain`), or whose measure cannot be merged (`preaggregate-not-mergeable`). Also two persisted views that resolve to one table, while `PERSIST_COLLISION_ENFORCE` is on (the default). Each fails the publish and the load, a package already published included (see "an invalid materialization annotation fails the load, everywhere" above).
  - **Refused at load.** An invalid incremental refresh policy on a `#(materialize)` source or a persisted view, such as `refresh="incremental"` with no `watermark=`. This is the rule a v1 `#@ persist` source has always been held to, and as for one, the package fails to load: a package already published, or loaded from a control plane's storage, stops loading until it is fixed. An incremental declaration on a dialect incremental refresh does not support refuses that source alone instead (see above).

  Before upgrading, load each package that carries a v2 annotation or a persisted view on a server with `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE=true` and fix what it reports, or set `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE=false` (below) until you have. Packages with only v1 annotations on sources and measures are not refused by this change. The release policy counts a refused package as breaking; whether this ships in a minor or a patch release is the release cutter's call.

- **Answers.** A query no table can answer is answered live, as before; the path report says which table a query read, and a `served-copy-not-served` warning says why a built source is not read. A persisted view's answer carries live's measure kinds, or is answered live (see "a persisted view's answer reports its measures as measures" above).

To opt out, set `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE=false`: `#(materialize)` and `#(preaggregate)` are ignored again and the build plan is what it was before. Set it the same on every worker, and treat it as one-way in an environment: once on, leave it on rather than switching it off and back on.

The setting is removed one release after this one, together with its off position; from then on materialization v2 is always on. See docs/materialization.md and docs/materialization-migration.md.

## [0.14.0] — a persisted view's date truncation reads back as a date

A query answered from a `storage=` persisted view's table (`#@ persist storage=…` on a `view:`, with `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE` on) declared each column as the type the table stored. A build stores each column as its declared type where it can, but one that declines that cast (a view or source with a query time zone) or retries without casts after one fails stores a date truncation such as `order_date.month` as a TIMESTAMP, and the answer then typed it `timestamp` where live types it `date`. The view leg now reads such a column through the served copy's faithful cast (`::"DATE"`, truncated again to its timeframe; an integer flag as `boolean`), so the column's type matches live; a column no faithful cast reads as live's type answers live. No table is rebuilt or re-addressed, and no API change.

## [0.14.0] — a stored table's zoned truncations and big integers read back with live's values

Several answers read from a stored table returned values near live's rather than live's own. Each now returns live's value, or is answered live:

- **A timestamp truncation under a time zone (persisted view).** A `storage=` persisted view whose view or source sets `timezone:` stored each truncation as the zone's midnight, as live computes it, but the read truncated the stored value again in UTC, so `created_at.day` under `timezone: 'America/New_York'` came back at 00:00Z where live answers 04:00Z. A later stage over such a view truncated in UTC on a colocated table too. The view leg now writes the view's and the source's zones where live has them, so the read truncates in the same zone the build did.
- **A timestamp truncation through the served copy.** A `#@ persist` or `#(materialize)` table re-read each timestamp truncation by truncating its stored value again in the query's zone. That matches live only when the zone is the one the build used. It is now decided column by column, with the decline reason `TIME_ZONE` ("a timestamp truncation stored in another zone"):
  - **A source that sets a zone, in its query or on itself.** A zoned daily rollup such as `orders -> { timezone: 'America/New_York'; group_by: created_at.day }` now answers live for any query that reads the truncated column. It stays served for one that does not, such as a total.
  - **A table with no zone.** A query that reads a truncation in another zone answers live. That zone is either one its own `timezone:` sets, or one the source it runs on sets or inherits (`ny is daily extend { timezone: … }`, which was served wrong before). A query in another zone that reads no truncation stays served, and an explicit `timezone: 'UTC'` counts as the default it is. The same rule now decides a stored computed dimension and a rolling window's cut-off. There, a query's own `timezone:` declines only when it differs from the zone the table was built in, so an explicit `'UTC'` over a default-zone table, or a source's own zone over a table built in that zone, stays served.
- **A BIGINT above 2^53 (persisted view).** A `storage=` persisted view declared a 64-bit integer column, dimension or measure, as a plain `number`, so 9007199254740993 came back as 9007199254740992. It is now read as `HUGEINT`, as the served copy reads one, and keeps every digit. A column stored as a float, which has lost digits already, is answered live.
- **A TIMESTAMP_NS, or another value live answers as warehouse-native or JSON (persisted view).** A `storage=` read declared it a `timestamp` and dropped its digits past the millisecond. Such a view is now answered live.
- **An `index:` view (persisted view).** Its stored read gave every column a `#(malloy)` annotation live does not write. It is now answered live, from either tier.

The stored contents were already right in every case, so no table is rebuilt or re-addressed. No API change.

## [0.14.0] — (BREAKING) `partition=` is no longer supported, and a publish that carries it is refused

`partition=` laid a `storage=` table out as one directory per value of the named columns. It is
removed from both `#@ persist` and `#(materialize)`, and a package that declares it is now
**refused at publish**: a package with `partition=` that published yesterday does not publish today.

**What to do:** remove `partition=` from the annotation and publish again. The table is then written
unpartitioned. `partition=` was a layout and never isolation, since every term that scopes a caller is
re-applied at read either way, so the only cost is scan cost: a read filtered to one value of the
column reads the whole table. No answer changes.

- **The refusal.** On `#@ persist` (written `partition="…"`, as a list, or inside the key as
  `#@ persist { partition="…" }`) the package warning is `persist-retired-key`, severity `error`, and
  the publish is refused with "`partition=` is no longer read …; remove it: partition= is not
  supported". On `#(materialize)` it is the new code `materialize-retired-key`. Either way the
  publish **and the load** fail, a package already published included (see "an invalid
  materialization annotation fails the load, everywhere" above, which replaces the publish-only
  refusal this section first shipped with).
- **What a loaded package's next build does.** A `storage=` `#@ persist` source that declared
  `partition=` has a new address, since the layout was part of it: its next build writes a new,
  unpartitioned table, and the old one is reclaimed as any superseded generation is. A colocated
  `#@ persist` source that declared `partition=` was refused (`partition_without_storage`) and never
  built; it now builds, into its own warehouse. A `#@ persist` on a view that declares `partition=`
  stays unbuilt (`persist-view-not-built`), now with a message that says to remove it.
- **Control-plane operators: reseed partitioned incremental sources.** An incremental
  `storage=` source that declared `partition=` is measured under its old address, so its first
  instructed run after the upgrade fails with "measured under a different definition … set reseed".
  Run it once with `reseed` (`--reseed`) to rebuild it in full under the new address.
- **API.** `BuildPlan.sources[].partition` is deprecated and always absent. The three refusal
  reasons `partition_without_storage`, `partition_column_unknown` and
  `partition_column_not_public` stay in the `RefusedSource.reason` enum, so generated clients keep
  compiling, and are no longer produced.
- **Configuration.** `duckdb.partitionedWriteFlushThreshold`
  (`PUBLISHER_PARTITIONED_WRITE_FLUSH_THRESHOLD`) is removed. A config file that still sets it
  loads with the usual unknown-key warning; the variable is ignored.
- **Unchanged.** The admin API's table copy still keeps a copied table's partition spec and writes
  it in partition order, so a table an earlier `partition=` build laid out copies as before. No other
  source's address, build SQL or stored table changes.

## [0.14.0] — (BREAKING) a model that joins sources across origin connections fails to load, as Malloy says

Malloy refuses a join into a source on another connection (`join-connection-mismatch`), and refuses it for the whole file. With `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE` on, Publisher used to load such a model anyway, with the join and everything that read it left out, and answer queries through the join once both sides were stored in one storage destination. That rescue is removed: whatever the switch says, such a model fails to load.

**Who is affected:** a package whose own files join a source on one connection to a source on another, served with `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE` set to `true` before this release. It loaded before; it now fails to load. A server that never set the switch sees no change, since such a model never loaded there. The whole package fails, its other models included, since a package's load stops at its first model that does not compile; the other packages in the environment load and serve as before. The load error is Malloy's own diagnostic (`Cannot join 'u', which is on connection 'product', into a source on connection 'crm'`): a `/status` `loadErrors` entry naming the package at boot, and a `424` from a publish.

**The fix:** put the joined sources on one connection.

Not affected: a stored source whose reference join reads a source that is not stored in its destination. The served copy still leaves that join out, so the queries that do not use it read the table, and a query that does is answered live (path report `CROSS_CONNECTION`, warning reason `cross_connection_join`). The `served-copy-not-served` warnings that named what a cross-connection model loaded without are gone with the rescue. No API change.

## [0.14.0] — the materialization rewriters read Malloy as Malloy reads it

The served copy and a build's copy of the author's files both rewrite the author's text, and read it with their own small lexer. That lexer now shares one core with the reader of a caller's query text, which follows Malloy's own lexer exactly. What changes:

- **Names in any script are read as names.** A source, field or join named outside ASCII (`café`, `größe`, `注文`) was split by the old lexer at its first non-ASCII letter, so its re-root on a stored table did not compile and the source answered live, with the package warning `served-copy-not-served` (`reroot_not_compiled`) and a serve verdict of `live`. Such a source is now served from its table, with the same answers. To tell whether you were affected: a stored source with a non-ASCII name whose serve verdict was `live` with that warning.
- **A string or quoted name ends at its line, a `#|` block annotation is skipped whole, and a `"""` block is one unit with the Malloy in its `%{ … }`.** None of these can be written differently in a model that compiles, so no compiled source's answers change. A text the rewriters read that holds a string crossing a line (which only a file edited since its last compile can) is now unreadable to them, and its source answers live rather than being rewritten around the break.

No API change. The reader of a caller's query text is unchanged: it accepts and rejects exactly what it did.

## [0.14.0] — `storage=` is read one way on every annotation, and an empty one refuses only its source

Every annotation that asks for a table now reads its destination by one rule: `#@ persist`, `#@ persist` on a view, `#@ preaggregate`, `#(materialize)` and `#(preaggregate)`. Two things change.

**`storage=` written inside the key is honoured everywhere.** `#@ persist { storage="lake" }` (and `name=` written the same way) now places the table exactly as `#@ persist storage="lake"` does. Before, a v1 `#@ persist` ignored the nested form and built in the source's own warehouse, and a persisted view written that way was built in the warehouse while its serve side looked for it in the destination, so it was never served. Who is affected: a package that writes the nested form on a v1 `#@ persist` or on a persisted view. Their tables now build into the destination, a one-time rebuild into a new place; until they are built there they answer live, with the same answers. Their content address and compiler key do not change (both come from the build's SQL, which is the same); with `PUBLISHER_PERSIST_ADDRESS_INCLUDES_DESTINATION` on, the address moves, as any move to `storage=` does. Run a build with `forceRefresh` if a skip-unchanged run does not rebuild them. The build plan's `annotationFields` for such a source now carry `storage` and `name`. A `#@ preaggregate` and a persisted view's serve side already read the nested form, and are unchanged.

**A `storage=` that names nothing refuses that source alone.** A `storage=` that is empty or only whitespace (`storage=""`), or that is not text at all (a list or a block), is now a refusal of that source or rollup, with a package warning saying why; the rest of the package loads and serves as usual, and the refused source answers live. That includes a source that shares the refused one's SQL, and so its table: it still builds and serves. Written inside the key, such a `storage=` refuses the source even when a usable `storage=` is also written beside the key, since the form inside the key always wins. Any other text is a destination name, looked up exactly; one that is not configured is unchanged: not built, answered live, with the `destination_missing` warning. Before, a v1 `#@ persist`, a `#(materialize)` and a persisted view built in the source's own warehouse instead, and a `#@ preaggregate` failed the whole package's load. Who is affected: a package with an empty `storage=`. A `#@ persist` source refused this way is listed in the build plan's `refusedSources` with the new reason `empty_storage` (warning code `persist-source-refused`); a `#(materialize)` warns `materialize-not-built`, a persisted view `persist-view-not-built`, and a `#@ preaggregate` rollup `preaggregate-malformed`. The one exception is a `#(preaggregate)` with an empty `storage=`: it is not refused alone, it fails the publish (`preaggregate-malformed`, severity `error`). Name the destination, or remove the key to build in the source's own warehouse. (Superseded in this same release: see "an invalid materialization annotation fails the load, everywhere" above, under which an empty `storage=` fails the publish and the load on every annotation.)

**API change.** `RefusedSource.reason` gains `empty_storage`. A client generated from an older spec that does not know the value sees an unknown enum value; Credible's control plane already tolerates unknown Publisher enum values, and should sync its copy of the spec when it next bumps. See docs/materialization.md, "Where a table is built".

## [0.14.0] — a stored source that inherits an `#(access_filter)` is no longer built

A source that reads an `#(access_filter)` row-level gate from a source it derives from or extends, rather than declaring the gate itself, is now refused at plan with reason `authorize` when it is marked for materialization. This covers a query over the gated source, an `extend` of it, a source two hops away, and the same across files. It applies to a colocated `#@ persist`, and, with `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE_GATED_SOURCES` on, to `#(materialize)`, colocated or `storage=`. Such a table held every caller's rows, but it was never read: the served copy cannot apply an inherited gate to a table that stands in for the source declaring it, so every query was declined and answered live. No answer changes. The build no longer spends warehouse time on these tables, and no longer leaves a copy of every caller's rows at rest. The refusal is listed in the build plan's `refusedSources` and in a run's `metadata.refusedSources`, with a message naming the inherited gate. To serve such a source from a table, declare the row-level gate on the source itself. The build plan also now lists as refused (reason `authorize`, or the refused source's own reason) a v1 colocated `#@ persist` source whose table another source refused for a colocated build shares (the same SQL, so one content address), such as an annotated join written beside a plain one. The build already refused it, and the bind served no source on that address, so the plan now says so instead of listing it as buildable. Downstreams that are served from their tables are unchanged: an annotated author join, an `#(authorize)` lock, a rollup with its base's gate grafted, and an `extend` over a given.

## [0.14.0] — a `storage=` table no column of which Malloy can type is built, and its source is answered live

A `storage=` build no longer compiles a per-build DuckDB check of the table it just wrote. Whether a stored table can be read is decided when it is bound, per source, by the served copy's own type plan, the one declaration rule every stored table follows. The one outcome that changes: a table none of whose columns Malloy has a faithful type for (every column a MAP, UNION, ENUM, BLOB, BIT, INTERVAL or JSON, or the table has no column at all) used to fail its build with a 422 whose `reason` was `not_duckdb_portable`. It now builds, and the served copy declines its source at bind (`column_types` in the package's `served-copy-not-served` warning), so every query over it is answered live, with the same answer as before. A table with at least one typed column builds and serves exactly as before. `not_duckdb_portable` stays in the API's reason enum, which is an open string, and is no longer produced. Each left-out column is still counted in `publisher_storage_serve_shape_type_fallback_total` and logged when its table is built.

v1 chained `storage=` builds (a `#@ persist storage=` source over another one in its destination) now compile from the author's own files with each stored parent re-rooted as a query reads it, not from a model the build assembled out of lifted text. What they build, and when they stack on a parent or recompute it, is unchanged. No API change.

## [0.14.0] — Bun 1.4.4: a respawned package-load worker no longer leaks its memory

Publisher now builds, tests and ships on Bun 1.4.4, up from 1.3.13. The Docker image's base is `oven/bun:1.4.4-slim`, and building from a clone needs Bun 1.4.4 or newer (`engines.bun` is now `>=1.4.4`). Running the published package with `npx` still needs only Node.js 20 or newer.

Bun 1.3 kept most of a worker thread's memory after the worker exited: about 78 MB of committed memory per worker on Windows, and a few MB on macOS and Linux. The package-load pool replaces a worker that timed out or crashed, so a long-running server that hit timeouts or crashes grew with each replacement. On Bun 1.4.4 that memory is returned. Over 60 worker spawn-and-shutdown cycles, a Windows runner grew from 0.28 to 5.8 GB on Bun 1.3.13 and stayed between 0.09 and 0.42 GB on Bun 1.4.4. The lockfile format is unchanged.

The image now declares a `HEALTHCHECK` against `/api/v0/status`: healthy while the server answers queries (`serving`, or `throttled`), with a 90-second start period, on the port in `PUBLISHER_PORT` (default 4000). `docker ps` and Compose report it; Kubernetes ignores it and keeps its own probes. If you start the server on another port by overriding the command with `--port`, set `PUBLISHER_PORT` to match or override the check.

## [0.13.1] — a field read inside a classified record or array column carries the column's classes

A field read inside a record or array column, such as `group_by: purchases.ssn` where `purchases` is a classified array (`#(classification) "phi.direct_identifier" rename: purchases is items`), was read with no classes at all. The access record listed it with `classifications: []` while still claiming a complete field list, so a source with no `#(carries)` under-reported what the query read. Under `#(carries)` the same read was refused as unclassified, even where the ceiling lists the column's class.

Now such a field carries the classes of the nearest record or array column around it that declares some, unless it declares its own. The access record lists `purchases.ssn` as `phi.direct_identifier`, a `#(carries)` ceiling that lists that class serves it, and one that does not refuses it naming the class. An element field read inside a query on the array (`purchases -> { select: ssn }`) carries the array's class the same way, and a read of the whole column still lists only the column. A record or array built by an expression already handed its parts its class and is unchanged.

## [0.13.1] — A pair table serves its counts again, and no longer serves a sum over a NULL or repeated child key

Behind `PUBLISHER_MATERIALIZE`, a pair table (`inline=` on a `join_many`) answers most of the counts 0.13.0 sent live (materialization v2 known limitation 40, narrowed). Since Malloy 0.0.438 live counts a parent with no child as none, where the pair table keeps one null-extended row for it. The served copy now re-declares each measure that counts through the inlined path, at its last join or at a flagged middle level (`seg_n is segments.count()`, a filtered count, a ratio over one), or sums or averages a value that is not a stored column there (`segments.sum(1)`, `segments.sum(segments.miles ?? 0)`, `segments.avg(1)`, `segments.sum(distance)`, a stored computed field), over the rows where that level's stored key is not null, as live's own guard reads them. Those measures, and the views, nests and queries that read them, are answered from the table again, equal to live on DuckDB and Postgres.

Two wrong answers are fixed on the way, both answered live now:

- **A NULL or repeated child key.** Live skips a child whose key is NULL in a `count()`, `sum` or `avg` through the join, and counts two equal children of one key twice; the pair table held the first as a row like any other and stored the second as one row, so even a stored column's sum (`segments.miles.sum()`) could come out wrong. Each auto-run build now checks the last join's key, unique and never NULL, over its joined source once the table is written. The check never fails the build: it is recorded beside the table, and every `count()`, `sum` and `avg` at the last join is served only where it passed. A table with no record (an orchestrated build, or one a host's manifest binds) answers those live; `min`, `max` and distinct counts are served as before.
- **A sum of a stored computed child field** written in the query (`segments.doubled.sum()`), whose value need not be NULL on a childless parent's row, was served from a one-join table; it is answered live (`COUNT_SEMANTICS`), and a measure declaring it is served over the key.

Still answered live (`COUNT_SEMANTICS`): a count, or a sum or average of such a value, written in the query or in a view's own `aggregate:` (`aggregate: n is segments.count()`) rather than in a measure, and a measure that pairs one with a `min` or `max` of a value not NULL on that row. Declare the count as a measure to have it served. No API change. See docs/materialization.md, "The served copy".

## [0.13.1] — Security: a join inside a query on an array is refused where a model governs access

Only a model that opts in to Malloy's experimental query on an array (`##! experimental.array_queries`, Malloy 0.0.438) is affected. The query on the array's elements (`items -> { … }`) can declare a join in an `extend:`, and nothing Publisher checks followed that join to the source it reads: Malloy's own field usage keeps only the elements' reads, and the load-time and per-query join walks do not look inside an expression. A model field or view written that way read a `#(carries)` source's fields past its list, at load and per query, and joined a gated source with no `join-bypass` warning, so a compliance review's `loads:join` check passed it; the access record listed the field with no classes. A caller could not exploit it, since the join has to be in the model: a caller's own such join was already refused where a gate or a `#(carries)` applies. A model that declares any `#(authorize)`, `#(access_filter)`, `#(carries)` or `#(classification)` now refuses the join: the package load fails with a 400 naming each join and its line, and a caller's query that writes one answers 400. A model that declares none of them serves it as before. An array query that reads only its elements is unaffected, and is now read correctly: a field inside it is read under its array (`items.price`, not `price`), so the access record no longer lists a field of the row the query never read, and a `#(carries)` source no longer refuses a dimension like `items -> { aggregate: t is price.sum() }` as unresolvable. Gates hold only behind the authenticating gateway that sets the givens ([docs/security-posture.md](docs/security-posture.md#operating-model-a-microservice-behind-your-gateway)).

## [0.13.1] — `storage=` tables with list, struct, MAP, BLOB, INTERVAL, ENUM, UNION or JSON columns build again
